verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — A Feast and a Hand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Belshazzar and his lords drink from the temple vessels while praising their idols, and a hand writes on the wall that none of his wise men can read (vv. 1-9).
verseByVerse.theology: God will not be mocked, and his judgment can interrupt the proudest celebration in an instant.

verseByVerse.quote: King Belshazzar made a great feast for a thousand of his lords and drank wine in front of the thousand. Belshazzar, when he tasted the wine, commanded that the vessels of gold and of silver that Nebuchadnezzar his father had taken out of the temple in Jerusalem be brought, that the king and his lords, his wives, and his concubines might drink from them. Then they brought in the golden vessels that had been taken out of the temple, the house of God in Jerusalem, and the king and his lords, his wives, and his concubines drank from them. They drank wine and praised the gods of gold and silver, bronze, iron, wood, and stone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Chapter 5 jumps forward more than twenty years. Nebuchadnezzar died in 562 BC, and several short reigns followed. By now the last king of Babylon was a man named Nabonidus, who spent years away from the capital. He left his son Belshazzar in charge of the city. So Belshazzar ruled Babylon, but under his father.

The date is October 539 BC. The armies of the Medes and Persians, led by Cyrus, were already in the region and had defeated Babylon's forces nearby. And in the city, Belshazzar threw a party. Ancient historians later recorded that Babylon fell while its people were celebrating a festival.

The words when he tasted the wine matter. The drink loosened whatever restraint he had left. He called for the sacred vessels from God's temple, the same ones we saw carried to Babylon in 1:2. For almost seventy years they had sat in a treasury. Now the king used them as party cups.

The ESV notes that father can also mean "predecessor". In the ancient world a king often called an earlier king his "father" even when they were not closely related. Nebuchadnezzar was Belshazzar's great predecessor on the throne of Babylon.

This was not merely bad manners. It was deliberate contempt. They drank from the vessels of the living God while praising idols. With an enemy army at the gates, Belshazzar chose to mock the God who rules history.

The prophets had seen this night coming. Isaiah described Babylon's leaders at a feast: They prepare the table, they spread the rugs, they eat, they drink. Arise, O princes; oil the shield! (Isa 21:5). And Jeremiah said that God would punish Babylon with the vengeance for his temple (Jer 51:11). Do not be deceived: God is not mocked, for whatever one sows, that will he also reap (Gal 6:7).
verseByVerse.note: Belshazzar’s name means “Bel, protect the king”.

verseByVerse.quote: Immediately the fingers of a human hand appeared and wrote on the plaster of the wall of the king's palace, opposite the lampstand. And the king saw the hand as it wrote. Then the king's color changed, and his thoughts alarmed him; his limbs gave way, and his knees knocked together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Immediately. God did not wait. In the middle of the laughter, a hand appeared, just the fingers of a hand, and began to write on the wall.

The proud king's face went white. His legs gave out. His knees knocked together. A few moments before he was mocking the God of Israel. Now he could not stand up. That is how quickly human arrogance collapses when God acts. It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God (Heb 10:31).

verseByVerse.quote: The king called loudly to bring in the enchanters, the Chaldeans, and the astrologers. The king declared to the wise men of Babylon, "Whoever reads this writing, and shows me its interpretation, shall be clothed with purple and have a chain of gold around his neck and shall be the third ruler in the kingdom." Then all the king's wise men came in, but they could not read the writing or make known to the king the interpretation. Then King Belshazzar was greatly alarmed, and his color changed, and his lords were perplexed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The frightened king offers enormous rewards: royal purple, a gold chain and a place as the third ruler in the kingdom. Why third and not second? Because Belshazzar himself was only second. His father Nabonidus was still the king. The best Belshazzar could offer was the next place below himself. This small detail fits exactly what we know of Babylon's history in its final years. For a long time critics doubted that Belshazzar had ever existed, since later Greek historians do not name him. Babylonian texts found since the nineteenth century name him as Nabonidus's son, entrusted with the kingship in Babylon.

For the third time in the book, Babylon's wise men fail (2:10-11; 4:7). They could not even read the words, let alone explain them. All the learning of Babylon was useless in the one moment it was needed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–16 — There Is a Man in Your Kingdom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The queen reminds the king of Daniel, in whom Nebuchadnezzar found light and understanding and wisdom like the wisdom of the gods (vv. 10-12). Daniel is brought in, and the king repeats his offer of honours if he can read the writing and interpret it (vv. 13-16).
verseByVerse.theology: God's faithful servant may be forgotten by the powerful, but he is not forgotten by God.

verseByVerse.quote: The queen, because of the words of the king and his lords, came into the banqueting hall, and the queen declared, "O king, live forever! Let not your thoughts alarm you or your color change. There is a man in your kingdom in whom is the spirit of the holy gods. In the days of your father, light and understanding and wisdom like the wisdom of the gods were found in him, and King Nebuchadnezzar, your father—your father the king— made him chief of the magicians, enchanters, Chaldeans, and astrologers, because an excellent spirit, knowledge, and understanding to interpret dreams, explain riddles, and solve problems were found in this Daniel, whom the king named Belteshazzar. Now let Daniel be called, and he will show the interpretation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ESV notes that queen may mean "queen mother". That fits well. Belshazzar's wives were already at the feast (v. 2), but this woman comes in from outside, hearing the uproar, and she remembers the days of Nebuchadnezzar. She was likely an older woman of the royal family who had known that earlier reign.

There is a man in your kingdom. The king did not know Daniel. The man who once ruled the province of Babylon and served Nebuchadnezzar for decades was no longer among the king's trusted advisers. He may still have held some lesser office, for in Belshazzar's third year he was still going about the king's business (8:27). But the new rulers had pushed him to the edges, and Belshazzar had forgotten him. The queen remembered.

God's servants are often forgotten by the powerful. Faithful people spend years out of the spotlight. But God knows exactly where they are, and when he needs them, he brings them back.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Daniel was brought in before the king. The king answered and said to Daniel, "You are that Daniel, one of the exiles of Judah, whom the king my father brought from Judah. I have heard of you that the spirit of the gods is in you, and that light and understanding and excellent wisdom are found in you. Now the wise men, the enchanters, have been brought in before me to read this writing and make known to me its interpretation, but they could not show the interpretation of the matter. But I have heard that you can give interpretations and solve problems. Now if you can read the writing and make known to me its interpretation, you shall be clothed with purple and have a chain of gold around your neck and shall be the third ruler in the kingdom."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Daniel is now an old man, probably in his eighties. And Belshazzar greets him as one of the exiles of Judah. Even after a lifetime of service, to this king Daniel is still a foreign captive. There may be a sneer in the words.

The king repeats his offer. He believes that anyone can be bought. He has spent the evening treating holy things as if they were his to use as he pleased. Now he assumes God's servant has a price too.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — You Have Not Humbled Your Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Daniel refuses the king's gifts, reminds him how God humbled Nebuchadnezzar, and charges him with refusing to humble his heart though he knew all this (vv. 17-24).
verseByVerse.theology: To sin against the light we have been given is a grave sin.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Daniel answered and said before the king, "Let your gifts be for yourself, and give your rewards to another. Nevertheless, I will read the writing to the king and make known to him the interpretation. O king, the Most High God gave Nebuchadnezzar your father kingship and greatness and glory and majesty. And because of the greatness that he gave him, all peoples, nations, and languages trembled and feared before him. Whom he would, he killed, and whom he would, he kept alive; whom he would, he raised up, and whom he would, he humbled. But when his heart was lifted up and his spirit was hardened so that he dealt proudly, he was brought down from his kingly throne, and his glory was taken from him. He was driven from among the children of mankind, and his mind was made like that of a beast, and his dwelling was with the wild donkeys. He was fed grass like an ox, and his body was wet with the dew of heaven, until he knew that the Most High God rules the kingdom of mankind and sets over it whom he will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Daniel's reply is blunt. Let your gifts be for yourself. He is not rude, but he is not interested. His message is not for sale. The prophet Elisha refused Naaman's gifts in the same way: As the LORD lives, before whom I stand, I will receive none (2 Kgs 5:16). And Jesus told his disciples, You received without paying; give without pay (Matt 10:8). A servant of God who can be bought cannot be trusted to tell the truth.

Besides, Daniel knew something the king did not. By morning Babylon's honours would be worthless.

Before Daniel reads the writing, he preaches. He begins with history. Nebuchadnezzar was the greatest king of his age, with the power of life and death over everyone. But all of it was given to him by the Most High God.

Nebuchadnezzar learned that lesson, and he was restored.

verseByVerse.quote: And you his son, Belshazzar, have not humbled your heart, though you knew all this, but you have lifted up yourself against the Lord of heaven. And the vessels of his house have been brought in before you, and you and your lords, your wives, and your concubines have drunk wine from them. And you have praised the gods of silver and gold, of bronze, iron, wood, and stone, which do not see or hear or know, but the God in whose hand is your breath, and whose are all your ways, you have not honored. "Then from his presence the hand was sent, and this writing was inscribed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the charge that seals Belshazzar's fate: though you knew all this. He was not ignorant. He knew what had happened to Nebuchadnezzar. The story had been proclaimed to the whole empire (4:1). He had the warning, and he ignored it. (The ESV notes that son can mean "successor", just as father can mean predecessor.)

Sinning in ignorance is serious. Sinning against knowledge is worse. Jesus said, Everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required (Luke 12:48). That should sober everyone who has grown up hearing the gospel: knowing the truth does not save; humbling ourselves before the God who offers mercy does. Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts (Heb 3:15).

Daniel names the sins: pride against God, contempt for holy things and the worship of idols that do not see or hear or know. And then he puts his finger on the deepest sin of all: the God in whose hand is your breath... you have not honored.

Every breath Belshazzar took that night, every mouthful of wine and every word of praise to his idols, was given to him by the God he mocked. That is true of every human being. God himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything (Acts 17:25). The heart of sin is not only doing bad things. It is living on God's gifts while refusing to honour the giver.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–31 — MENE, MENE, TEKEL, and PARSIN
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The writing is interpreted: God has numbered the days of the kingdom; you have been weighed in the balances and found wanting; the kingdom is divided and given to the Medes and Persians (vv. 25-28). Daniel is honoured as third ruler (v. 29). That very night Belshazzar the Chaldean king was killed, and Darius the Mede received the kingdom (vv. 30-31).
verseByVerse.theology: God weighs every life, and his word of judgment comes true exactly as he says.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is the writing that was inscribed: MENE, MENE, TEKEL, and PARSIN. This is the interpretation of the matter: MENE, God has numbered the days of your kingdom and brought it to an end; TEKEL, you have been weighed in the balances and found wanting; PERES, your kingdom is divided and given to the Medes and Persians."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The words on the wall were short, and each one was a kind of pun. The ESV's notes explain the wordplay: each word sounds like a verb that carries part of the message.

MENE sounds like the Aramaic word for "numbered". God had counted Belshazzar's days, and the last one had arrived. Every kingdom, and every life, has a number of days, and God knows the number. The word is written twice, perhaps for emphasis: it is certain.

TEKEL sounds like the word for "weighed". Picture a merchant's scale, with a weight on one side. God put Belshazzar on the scale, and he was too light. Found wanting means he did not measure up. He was all show and no substance. By him actions are weighed (1 Sam 2:3). In the balances they go up; they are together lighter than a breath (Ps 62:9).

This is the most searching sentence in the chapter, because it is true of all of us. If God put any of us on his scale, we would be found wanting. For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Rom 3:23). The only hope for anyone weighed by God is to have another's weight placed on the scale. That is the gospel. For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Cor 5:21). Paul's great desire was to be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own (Phil 3:9). In Christ, those who were found wanting are found complete.

PERES is the singular form of PARSIN, and the ESV notes that it sounds like both "divided" and "Persia". The kingdom is being broken up, and it is being handed to the Persians. The message was not a warning with time to repent. It was a verdict.
verseByVerse.note: Many scholars note that the three words are also names of weights: a mina, a shekel (tekel) and half-minas (parsin).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Belshazzar gave the command, and Daniel was clothed with purple, a chain of gold was put around his neck, and a proclamation was made about him, that he should be the third ruler in the kingdom. That very night Belshazzar the Chaldean king was killed. And Darius the Mede received the kingdom, being about sixty-two years old.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Strangely, Belshazzar keeps his word and honours Daniel. But he shows no sign of repentance. He treats the message of God's judgment as a clever puzzle solved, not as a call to his knees. Daniel accepted the honours he had not asked for, but they would last only a few hours.

The Medes and Persians entered the city that night, and Babylon, the head of gold, fell almost without a battle. The king who began the evening mocking God did not live to see the morning. The prophets had foretold it: Fallen, fallen is Babylon (Isa 21:9). Jeremiah had written that God would make Babylon's leaders drunk so that they would sleep a perpetual sleep and not wake (Jer 51:57).

Chapters 4 and 5 stand side by side on purpose. Two kings were both proud, and both were warned. One humbled himself and was restored. The other did not and was destroyed. He who is often reproved, yet stiffens his neck, will suddenly be broken beyond healing (Prov 29:1). The difference between them was not the size of their sins. It was what they did with God's warning. Behold, now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation (2 Cor 6:2).

A new ruler takes over Babylon. Who was Darius the Mede? No other ancient record we have mentions a ruler by that name, so Christians have offered different suggestions. Some think he was Gubaru, the governor Cyrus set over Babylon, or Ugbaru, the general who took the city; Daniel calls him one who was made king (9:1), as a vassal is. Others take 6:28 to mean "Darius, that is, Cyrus", so that Darius the Mede is another title for Cyrus. Many critical scholars think the writer confused later traditions about the Persian king Darius I. This commentary takes Darius the Mede as a real ruler, but we do not have enough evidence to be certain who he was. What matters is that the kingdom passed exactly as the writing on the wall said it would, to the Medes and Persians.

And Daniel, the old exile, was still there. Babylon had fallen. The king who mocked God was dead. But God's servant was still standing. As 1:21 promised, Daniel was there, and the empire was not.
verseByVerse.note: Babylon fell to the Medes and Persians in October 539 BC. Daniel 5:31 is 6:1 in Aramaic (ESV note).

5.title: Weighed and Found Wanting
5.overview: On the last night of Babylon, King Belshazzar drinks from the vessels of God's temple while praising his idols, and a hand writes on the wall (vv. 1-9). The forgotten Daniel is brought in (vv. 10-16). He refuses the king's gifts, reminds him how God humbled Nebuchadnezzar, and charges him with pride against the God who holds his breath (vv. 17-24). The writing means that the king has been weighed and found wanting, and that very night Babylon falls (vv. 25-31). Chapter 4 showed a proud king who humbled himself; chapter 5 shows one who would not.
5.theology:
God is not mocked; contempt for what is holy brings his judgment, as the prophets foretold (vv. 1-6; Gal 6:7; Isa 21:5, 9; Jer 51:11, 57; Heb 10:31).

God's servants may be forgotten by the powerful but are kept by God for his purposes (vv. 10-13).

God's message cannot be bought (v. 17; 2 Kgs 5:16; Matt 10:8).

To sin against knowledge is especially serious; those who have heard the warnings must humble themselves (v. 22; Luke 12:48; Heb 3:15; Prov 29:1).

Every human being lives on God's gifts of life and breath and owes him honour (v. 23; Acts 17:25).

God numbers and weighs every life; all are found wanting, and the only hope is the righteousness of God in Christ (vv. 26-27; Rom 3:23; 2 Cor 5:21; Phil 3:9).

God's word of judgment comes true exactly as spoken, and kingdoms pass as he decrees (vv. 28, 30-31; 2 Cor 6:2).
5.examples: Belshazzar partied while an enemy army waited outside, and many still fill their lives with noise to avoid thinking about the God who will weigh them. The writing on the wall is not only a verdict on him. It is a warning to everyone who has heard the story of God's mercy and judgment and has not yet humbled their heart. The way to stand on God's scale is to stand in Christ.

6.text: <sup>1</sup>It pleased Darius to set over the kingdom 120 satraps, to be throughout the whole kingdom;<sup>2</sup>and over them three high officials, of whom Daniel was one, to whom these satraps should give account, so that the king might suffer no loss.<sup>3</sup>Then this Daniel became distinguished above all the other high officials and satraps, because an excellent spirit was in him. And the king planned to set him over the whole kingdom.<sup>4</sup>Then the high officials and the satraps sought to find a ground for complaint against Daniel with regard to the kingdom, but they could find no ground for complaint or any fault, because he was faithful, and no error or fault was found in him.<sup>5</sup>Then these men said, "We shall not find any ground for complaint against this Daniel unless we find it in connection with the law of his God."<sup>6</sup>Then these high officials and satraps came by agreement to the king and said to him, "O King Darius, live forever!<sup>7</sup>All the high officials of the kingdom, the prefects and the satraps, the counselors and the governors are agreed that the king should establish an ordinance and enforce an injunction, that whoever makes petition to any god or man for thirty days, except to you, O king, shall be cast into the den of lions.<sup>8</sup>Now, O king, establish the injunction and sign the document, so that it cannot be changed, according to the law of the Medes and the Persians, which cannot be revoked."<sup>9</sup>Therefore King Darius signed the document and injunction.<sup>10</sup>When Daniel knew that the document had been signed, he went to his house where he had windows in his upper chamber open toward Jerusalem. He got down on his knees three times a day and prayed and gave thanks before his God, as he had done previously.<sup>11</sup>Then these men came by agreement and found Daniel making petition and plea before his God.<sup>12</sup>Then they came near and said before the king, concerning the injunction, "O king! Did you not sign an injunction, that anyone who makes petition to any god or man within thirty days except to you, O king, shall be cast into the den of lions?" The king answered and said, "The thing stands fast, according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which cannot be revoked."<sup>13</sup>Then they answered and said before the king, "Daniel, who is one of the exiles from Judah, pays no attention to you, O king, or the injunction you have signed, but makes his petition three times a day."<sup>14</sup>Then the king, when he heard these words, was much distressed and set his mind to deliver Daniel. And he labored till the sun went down to rescue him.<sup>15</sup>Then these men came by agreement to the king and said to the king, "Know, O king, that it is a law of the Medes and Persians that no injunction or ordinance that the king establishes can be changed."<sup>16</sup>Then the king commanded, and Daniel was brought and cast into the den of lions. The king declared to Daniel, "May your God, whom you serve continually, deliver you!"<sup>17</sup>And a stone was brought and laid on the mouth of the den, and the king sealed it with his own signet and with the signet of his lords, that nothing might be changed concerning Daniel.<sup>18</sup>Then the king went to his palace and spent the night fasting; no diversions were brought to him, and sleep fled from him.<sup>19</sup>Then, at break of day, the king arose and went in haste to the den of lions.<sup>20</sup>As he came near to the den where Daniel was, he cried out in a tone of anguish. The king declared to Daniel, "O Daniel, servant of the living God, has your God, whom you serve continually, been able to deliver you from the lions?"<sup>21</sup>Then Daniel said to the king, "O king, live forever!<sup>22</sup>My God sent his angel and shut the lions' mouths, and they have not harmed me, because I was found blameless before him; and also before you, O king, I have done no harm."<sup>23</sup>Then the king was exceedingly glad, and commanded that Daniel be taken up out of the den. So Daniel was taken up out of the den, and no kind of harm was found on him, because he had trusted in his God.<sup>24</sup>And the king commanded, and those men who had maliciously accused Daniel were brought and cast into the den of lions—they, their children, and their wives. And before they reached the bottom of the den, the lions overpowered them and broke all their bones in pieces.<sup>25</sup>Then King Darius wrote to all the peoples, nations, and languages that dwell in all the earth: "Peace be multiplied to you.<sup>26</sup>I make a decree, that in all my royal dominion people are to tremble and fear before the God of Daniel, for he is the living God, enduring forever; his kingdom shall never be destroyed, and his dominion shall be to the end.<sup>27</sup>He delivers and rescues; he works signs and wonders in heaven and on earth, he who has saved Daniel from the power of the lions."<sup>28</sup>So this Daniel prospered during the reign of Darius and the reign of Cyrus the Persian.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Daniel serves so well that his jealous rivals can find no fault in him except his faith, so they persuade the king to sign a law against praying to anyone but the king (vv. 1-9).
verseByVerse.theology: A faithful life leaves enemies nothing to attack but its faith.

verseByVerse.quote: It pleased Darius to set over the kingdom 120 satraps, to be throughout the whole kingdom; and over them three high officials, of whom Daniel was one, to whom these satraps should give account, so that the king might suffer no loss. Then this Daniel became distinguished above all the other high officials and satraps, because an excellent spirit was in him. And the king planned to set him over the whole kingdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Babylon has fallen, and a new empire rules. The Medes and Persians organized their huge territory carefully. Satraps were provincial governors, each responsible for a region. Over these 120 governors Darius set three senior officials to keep watch on them, so that the king might suffer no loss (v. 2). In other words, their job was to stop corruption and make sure the taxes reached the king.

Daniel was now an old man, probably over eighty. He had served the kings of Babylon for most of his life. A new king might easily have removed the old regime's officials. God had kept Daniel through the fall of an empire and placed him again at the centre of power.

An excellent spirit includes ability but also character: wisdom, honesty and steadiness.

Daniel's faith did not make him a poor employee. It made him an outstanding one. Excellent, honest work in a secular job is one of the ways God's people honour the God who has placed them there.

This Darius is the Mede of 5:31, perhaps a ruler set over Babylon under Cyrus (5:31 discusses the options). The 120 satraps are more than the twenty or so great provinces of the later Persian empire, so the word is probably used here in a broader sense for regional officials, much as Esther counts 127 provinces (Esth 1:1).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the high officials and the satraps sought to find a ground for complaint against Daniel with regard to the kingdom, but they could find no ground for complaint or any fault, because he was faithful, and no error or fault was found in him. Then these men said, "We shall not find any ground for complaint against this Daniel unless we find it in connection with the law of his God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Success brought envy. The other officials probably did not want a foreign Jew promoted over them, and they may also have feared an honest man who would stop them from filling their own pockets. So they searched his work for anything they could use.

They found nothing: a lifetime of public service examined by enemies, and clean. Their own verdict was that they would find nothing unless we find it in connection with the law of his God. What a thing for enemies to say.

This is what Peter asks of Christians: Keep your conduct among the Gentiles honorable, so that when they speak against you as evildoers, they may see your good deeds (1 Pet 2:12). Paul tells Titus to live so that an opponent may be put to shame, having nothing evil to say about us (Titus 2:8). The world will still oppose believers. But let it be for their faith, not for their faults.

The only place they could attack Daniel was his devotion to God. None of us has a record like that before God; there is one whose record is wholly clean, and in Christ his righteousness is counted as ours (Phil 3:9). It is the Spirit he gives who then begins to make our conduct honourable in the world's sight.

parallels.desc: enemies watch Jesus to trap him

verseByVerse.quote: Then these high officials and satraps came by agreement to the king and said to him, "O King Darius, live forever! All the high officials of the kingdom, the prefects and the satraps, the counselors and the governors are agreed that the king should establish an ordinance and enforce an injunction, that whoever makes petition to any god or man for thirty days, except to you, O king, shall be cast into the den of lions. Now, O king, establish the injunction and sign the document, so that it cannot be changed, according to the law of the Medes and the Persians, which cannot be revoked." Therefore King Darius signed the document and injunction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ESV notes that came by agreement could also be translated "came thronging".

Their claim was a lie. All the high officials... are agreed. But there were only three high officials (v. 2), and one of them was Daniel, who had certainly not agreed. The conspirators flattered the king with a proposal that for thirty days he alone would receive prayers. To a new ruler it may have seemed harmless.

But the trap was set for one man. They knew Daniel's habit of prayer and built a law that would make his faithfulness a crime.

According to Daniel and Esther, the Persian court had a rule that once the king signed a law and sealed it, even he could not cancel it. Esther says: an edict written in the name of the king and sealed with the king's ring cannot be revoked (Esth 8:8). In practice the king could be trapped by his own word.

Flattery works. Darius signed without asking the obvious questions: who suggested this, and why? Leaders who love praise are easily used by those who give it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–15 — As He Had Done Previously
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Daniel goes on praying at his open window as he had done previously, and the king cannot undo his own law (vv. 10-15).
verseByVerse.theology: Faithful prayer is a steady habit, kept openly when it becomes costly.

verseByVerse.quote: When Daniel knew that the document had been signed, he went to his house where he had windows in his upper chamber open toward Jerusalem. He got down on his knees three times a day and prayed and gave thanks before his God, as he had done previously.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This one verse is the heart of the chapter, and every phrase matters. When Daniel knew. He was not caught unaware. He knew exactly what the law said and what it would cost.

He went to his house. He went where he always prayed. He neither staged a demonstration nor hid.

Windows in his upper chamber open toward Jerusalem. Why toward Jerusalem? Centuries earlier, when King Solomon dedicated the temple, he prayed that if Israel ever went into exile for their sins and prayed toward their land... the city that you have chosen, and the house that I have built for your name, God would hear them and forgive (1 Kgs 8:48-49). Jerusalem lay in ruins and the temple was gone, but Daniel was still leaning on God's promise to hear the prayers of his people in exile.

He got down on his knees three times a day. This was a settled rhythm of prayer, like the psalmist's: Evening and morning and at noon I utter my complaint and moan, and he hears my voice (Ps 55:17). His prayer life was built before the crisis came.

And prayed and gave thanks. With the lions waiting, Daniel gave thanks. Give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you (1 Thess 5:18).

As he had done previously. Daniel neither started nor stopped praying because of the crisis. Courage in the great moment grows out of faithfulness in ten thousand ordinary ones, and those ordinary prayers were themselves leaning on the God who had promised to hear.

Why did Daniel not simply close his windows or pray silently for thirty days? God hears silent prayers. But to change his lifelong habit at the moment the king demanded it would have been to accept that the king had authority over his worship. Daniel was a loyal servant of the king in everything else. Here he had to obey God rather than man. Jesus warned against praying in public that they may be seen by others (Matt 6:5). Daniel was not showing off. He was refusing to hide.

Should Christians face Jerusalem or keep set hours? Daniel faced Jerusalem because the temple was where God had promised to hear (1 Kgs 8:48–49). Now Jesus says true worshippers worship in spirit and truth, not on a mountain or in a city (John 4:21–24), and Christ is the place where we meet God (Heb 10:19–22). No direction or hour binds us. But Daniel’s steady habit of prayer, kept when it became dangerous, is a pattern every believer can follow.
verseByVerse.note: An upper room on the flat roof was a natural place for quiet prayer (compare Acts 10:9).

verseByVerse.quote: Then these men came by agreement and found Daniel making petition and plea before his God. Then they came near and said before the king, concerning the injunction, "O king! Did you not sign an injunction, that anyone who makes petition to any god or man within thirty days except to you, O king, shall be cast into the den of lions?" The king answered and said, "The thing stands fast, according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which cannot be revoked." Then they answered and said before the king, "Daniel, who is one of the exiles from Judah, pays no attention to you, O king, or the injunction you have signed, but makes his petition three times a day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The conspirators came together to watch, and they found exactly what they expected. Daniel was making petition and plea before his God.

They make the king confirm the law before naming Daniel. The thing stands fast, the king says, not yet knowing who it will catch.

Their words are full of contempt. They call him one of the exiles from Judah. And they accuse him of disrespecting the king, which is the same false charge made against his friends in 3:12.

Faithful believers are often accused of disloyalty when their only offence is loyalty to God. Jesus warned, If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you (John 15:20). Indeed, all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted (2 Tim 3:12).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king, when he heard these words, was much distressed and set his mind to deliver Daniel. And he labored till the sun went down to rescue him. Then these men came by agreement to the king and said to the king, "Know, O king, that it is a law of the Medes and Persians that no injunction or ordinance that the king establishes can be changed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the king understands what has happened. He has been tricked into condemning the man he trusted most. He is much distressed and spends the day seeking a legal way out.

At sunset the conspirators return and remind the king of his own law. His word has become a chain around him.

This scene has a striking parallel in the Gospels. Pilate, the Roman governor, knew that Jesus was innocent. I find no guilt in this man, he said (Luke 23:4). He tried again and again to release him, desiring to release Jesus (Luke 23:20). And like Darius, he knew why the accusers wanted him dead: it was out of envy that they had delivered him up (Matt 27:18). But in the end Pilate, too, gave in to the pressure. There is a great difference. Darius was trapped by a law. Pilate was trapped by his own cowardice. And behind both scenes stood the purposes of God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–24 — He Shut the Lions' Mouths
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Daniel is thrown to the lions and the den is sealed; at dawn the king finds him alive, because God shut the lions' mouths, and his accusers are thrown in instead (vv. 16-24).
verseByVerse.theology: God is able to deliver those who trust him, and his justice finally overtakes their enemies.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king commanded, and Daniel was brought and cast into the den of lions. The king declared to Daniel, "May your God, whom you serve continually, deliver you!" And a stone was brought and laid on the mouth of the den, and the king sealed it with his own signet and with the signet of his lords, that nothing might be changed concerning Daniel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A lions' den was probably a pit in the ground, with an opening at the top through which the victim was thrown.

The king's last words to Daniel are a mixture of hope and helplessness: May your God, whom you serve continually, deliver you! The king had noticed that Daniel served his God continually, and now pinned his hope on that God.

A stone was laid over the opening, and it was sealed. Wet clay stamped with the rings would show if the stone were moved. The seal of the lords meant the king could not secretly rescue Daniel. The seal of the king meant the lords could not secretly make sure he died. No human hand could interfere. The seal had a purpose its makers never intended: it proved that whatever happened in the den was God's doing alone.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king went to his palace and spent the night fasting; no diversions were brought to him, and sleep fled from him. Then, at break of day, the king arose and went in haste to the den of lions. As he came near to the den where Daniel was, he cried out in a tone of anguish. The king declared to Daniel, "O Daniel, servant of the living God, has your God, whom you serve continually, been able to deliver you from the lions?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The contrast is almost humorous. In the pit, Daniel was with the lions. In the palace, the king was the one who could not rest. The man in the den was in God's hands. The man on the throne was in torment.

The king calls out in anguish, afraid of the silence that might answer. But listen to how he now speaks of God: the living God. And his question is the question of the whole book: is this God able? Nebuchadnezzar had asked the same thing mockingly (3:15). Darius asks it in hope.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Daniel said to the king, "O king, live forever! My God sent his angel and shut the lions' mouths, and they have not harmed me, because I was found blameless before him; and also before you, O king, I have done no harm." Then the king was exceedingly glad, and commanded that Daniel be taken up out of the den. So Daniel was taken up out of the den, and no kind of harm was found on him, because he had trusted in his God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The voice from the pit is calm and courteous. Daniel greets the king who condemned him with respect and without bitterness. Like his Lord after him, When he was reviled, he did not revile in return (1 Pet 2:23).

Daniel gives God all the credit: My God sent his angel. The lions were hungry (v. 24), and God himself closed their mouths. The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them (Ps 34:7). The book of Hebrews remembers Daniel among the heroes of faith who stopped the mouths of lions (Heb 11:33).

And Daniel declares his innocence twice: blameless before him, and before the king, I have done no harm. He had broken the king's law, but he had not wronged the king. Obeying God rather than man is not disloyalty. It is the only true loyalty.

As in the furnace, the deliverance was complete, and the writer tells us why: because he had trusted in his God. It was not because Daniel was an extraordinary man, though he was. It was because he trusted God. Without faith it is impossible to please him, for whoever would draw near to God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him (Heb 11:6).

We should be careful here. God does not promise that every faithful believer will be rescued from every lion. Many have died for their faith, and Hebrews honours them too. Paul, near the end of his life, could say, I was rescued from the lion's mouth, and in the next breath, The Lord will rescue me from every evil deed and bring me safely into his heavenly kingdom (2 Tim 4:17-18). He knew he would soon be executed. For the Christian, the final deliverance is always certain, whether God brings us out of the den in this life or through death into his presence.

Many Christians have seen in this story a pattern that points beyond itself. Daniel was innocent, condemned through envy, put into a pit, sealed in with a stone, and brought out alive at dawn. Jesus was innocent, condemned through envy, put into a tomb and sealed in with a stone, as his enemies made the tomb secure by sealing the stone and setting a guard (Matt 27:66). But Jesus was not spared death. He went all the way into it, bearing the sins of his people. And on the third day, early in the morning, the stone was rolled away and he came out alive, because it was not possible for him to be held by it (Acts 2:24). Daniel was delivered from death. Christ conquered it. That is why those who trust him are safe even in the den.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king commanded, and those men who had maliciously accused Daniel were brought and cast into the den of lions—they, their children, and their wives. And before they reached the bottom of the den, the lions overpowered them and broke all their bones in pieces.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This verse is hard to read. The accusers suffered the fate they had planned for Daniel, and that is justice. Scripture often describes the wicked falling into the pit they dug for others. The lions were clearly not tame or full: they seized the men before they reached the bottom of the den. Daniel's survival was no accident.

But the king also threw in their wives and children. That was the practice of ancient Persian kings, who often destroyed a traitor's whole family. The Bible records it; it does not approve it. God's law for Israel said plainly, nor shall children be put to death because of their fathers. Each one shall be put to death for his own sin (Deut 24:16). The terrible end of those families shows how deeply the sin of a few leaders can wound the people who depend on them, and it reminds us that the justice of human kings, even when it punishes real wrongdoing, is never the perfect justice of God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–28 — His Kingdom Shall Never Be Destroyed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Darius decrees that all his dominion must tremble before the God of Daniel, for he is the living God, enduring forever; his kingdom shall never be destroyed, the God who delivers and rescues (vv. 25-27). So this Daniel prospered during the reign of Darius and the reign of Cyrus the Persian (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology: The deliverance of one faithful servant proclaims the living God to the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: Then King Darius wrote to all the peoples, nations, and languages that dwell in all the earth: "Peace be multiplied to you. I make a decree, that in all my royal dominion people are to tremble and fear before the God of Daniel, for he is the living God, enduring forever; his kingdom shall never be destroyed, and his dominion shall be to the end. He delivers and rescues; he works signs and wonders in heaven and on earth, he who has saved Daniel from the power of the lions."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends with a pagan king writing to the whole world, as Nebuchadnezzar did in chapter 4. The thirty-day law demanded that everyone pray to the king. The new decree tells everyone to fear Daniel's God.

Darius's confession sounds very much like the message of the whole book. God is the living God, unlike the dead idols of the nations. He is enduring forever, while kings and empires come and go. His kingdom shall never be destroyed, almost the very words Daniel spoke to Nebuchadnezzar about the stone that fills the earth (2:44). And He delivers and rescues.

Daniel set out only to be faithful, and God made his quiet faithfulness a testimony across an empire.

verseByVerse.quote: So this Daniel prospered during the reign of Darius and the reign of Cyrus the Persian.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The historical half of the book ends with a quiet summary. Daniel prospered. The man who entered Babylon as a captive teenager outlived Nebuchadnezzar, saw Babylon fall, survived the lions and served the kings of Persia with honour.

Whether Darius and Cyrus are two rulers or two names for one king (see 5:31), the point is clear. Kings change. The faithful servant of God remains.

The first six chapters of Daniel have taught one lesson from many angles: the Most High rules, and he is able to keep those who trust him, even in Babylon. The rest of the book will lift our eyes to the future. The kingdoms of this world will grow more beastly and more hostile. But the lesson of the lions' den stands behind every vision. Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah... has conquered (Rev 5:5).

6.title: The Living God, Enduring Forever
6.overview: Daniel, now an old man, serves the new Persian rulers so faithfully that his jealous rivals can find no fault in him except his devotion to God, so they trap him with a law against prayer (vv. 1-9). He prays at his open window as he always had, and the king is forced by his own decree to condemn him (vv. 10-15). God shuts the lions' mouths, and Daniel comes out unharmed at dawn (vv. 16-24). Darius ends by proclaiming to the whole empire the living God, whose kingdom shall never be destroyed (vv. 25-28).
6.theology:
Believers honour God by excellent, honest work, so that opponents can find no fault but their faith (vv. 3-5; 1 Pet 2:12; Titus 2:7-8).

Faithful prayer is a settled habit that does not stop when it becomes costly; God's people obey God rather than men while remaining loyal servants in everything else (vv. 10, 22; 1 Kgs 8:48-49; Ps 55:17; 1 Thess 5:17-18).

The godly will be falsely accused and persecuted, as their Lord was (vv. 5, 13; John 15:20; 2 Tim 3:12; Matt 27:18).

God is able to deliver those who trust in him, and his final deliverance of his people is certain even when he does not spare them from death (vv. 22-23; Ps 34:7; Heb 11:6, 33; 2 Tim 4:17-18).

Many Christians have seen in Daniel's condemnation, sealed stone and dawn deliverance a foreshadowing of Christ, who was condemned through envy, sealed in a tomb and raised from death (vv. 14-23; Luke 23:4, 20; Matt 27:66; Acts 2:24).

Human justice, even when it punishes real wrong, falls short of God's perfect justice (v. 24; Deut 24:16).

The living God endures forever, his kingdom shall never be destroyed, and he delivers and rescues (vv. 26-27; 2:44; Rev 5:5).
6.examples: Daniel's courage at the window was built in years of ordinary prayer that no one noticed. A believer who keeps a daily time of prayer when life is calm is laying up strength for the day it becomes costly, whether that means praying openly at work, holding to Christ under family pressure, or simply giving thanks on the worst day of the year. If our prayer has been patchy, the way back is not resolve but the open window: the God who promised to hear is still listening.

7.text: <sup>1</sup>In the first year of Belshazzar king of Babylon, Daniel saw a dream and visions of his head as he lay in his bed. Then he wrote down the dream and told the sum of the matter.<sup>2</sup>Daniel declared, "I saw in my vision by night, and behold, the four winds of heaven were stirring up the great sea.<sup>3</sup>And four great beasts came up out of the sea, different from one another.<sup>4</sup>The first was like a lion and had eagles' wings. Then as I looked its wings were plucked off, and it was lifted up from the ground and made to stand on two feet like a man, and the mind of a man was given to it.<sup>5</sup>And behold, another beast, a second one, like a bear. It was raised up on one side. It had three ribs in its mouth between its teeth; and it was told, 'Arise, devour much flesh.'<sup>6</sup>After this I looked, and behold, another, like a leopard, with four wings of a bird on its back. And the beast had four heads, and dominion was given to it.<sup>7</sup>After this I saw in the night visions, and behold, a fourth beast, terrifying and dreadful and exceedingly strong. It had great iron teeth; it devoured and broke in pieces and stamped what was left with its feet. It was different from all the beasts that were before it, and it had ten horns.<sup>8</sup>I considered the horns, and behold, there came up among them another horn, a little one, before which three of the first horns were plucked up by the roots. And behold, in this horn were eyes like the eyes of a man, and a mouth speaking great things.<sup>9</sup>"As I looked, thrones were placed, and the Ancient of Days took his seat; his clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool; his throne was fiery flames; its wheels were burning fire.<sup>10</sup>A stream of fire issued and came out from before him; a thousand thousands served him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him; the court sat in judgment, and the books were opened.<sup>11</sup>"I looked then because of the sound of the great words that the horn was speaking. And as I looked, the beast was killed, and its body destroyed and given over to be burned with fire.<sup>12</sup>As for the rest of the beasts, their dominion was taken away, but their lives were prolonged for a season and a time.<sup>13</sup>"I saw in the night visions, and behold, with the clouds of heaven there came one like a son of man, and he came to the Ancient of Days and was presented before him.<sup>14</sup>And to him was given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him; his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom one that shall not be destroyed.<sup>15</sup>"As for me, Daniel, my spirit within me was anxious, and the visions of my head alarmed me.<sup>16</sup>I approached one of those who stood there and asked him the truth concerning all this. So he told me and made known to me the interpretation of the things.<sup>17</sup>'These four great beasts are four kings who shall arise out of the earth.<sup>18</sup>But the saints of the Most High shall receive the kingdom and possess the kingdom forever, forever and ever.'<sup>19</sup>"Then I desired to know the truth about the fourth beast, which was different from all the rest, exceedingly terrifying, with its teeth of iron and claws of bronze, and which devoured and broke in pieces and stamped what was left with its feet,<sup>20</sup>and about the ten horns that were on its head, and the other horn that came up and before which three of them fell, the horn that had eyes and a mouth that spoke great things, and that seemed greater than its companions.<sup>21</sup>As I looked, this horn made war with the saints and prevailed over them,<sup>22</sup>until the Ancient of Days came, and judgment was given for the saints of the Most High, and the time came when the saints possessed the kingdom.<sup>23</sup>"Thus he said: 'As for the fourth beast, there shall be a fourth kingdom on earth, which shall be different from all the kingdoms, and it shall devour the whole earth, and trample it down, and break it to pieces.<sup>24</sup>As for the ten horns, out of this kingdom ten kings shall arise, and another shall arise after them; he shall be different from the former ones, and shall put down three kings.<sup>25</sup>He shall speak words against the Most High, and shall wear out the saints of the Most High, and shall think to change the times and the law; and they shall be given into his hand for a time, times, and half a time.<sup>26</sup>But the court shall sit in judgment, and his dominion shall be taken away, to be consumed and destroyed to the end.<sup>27</sup>And the kingdom and the dominion and the greatness of the kingdoms under the whole heaven shall be given to the people of the saints of the Most High; his kingdom shall be an everlasting kingdom, and all dominions shall serve and obey him.'<sup>28</sup>"Here is the end of the matter. As for me, Daniel, my thoughts greatly alarmed me, and my color changed, but I kept the matter in my heart."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Four Beasts from the Sea
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Daniel sees four great beasts rise from the stormy sea, the fourth with iron teeth, ten horns and a boastful little horn (vv. 1-8).
verseByVerse.theology: Behind the glory of human empires lies a beastly, devouring power that sets itself against God.

verseByVerse.quote: In the first year of Belshazzar king of Babylon, Daniel saw a dream and visions of his head as he lay in his bed. Then he wrote down the dream and told the sum of the matter. Daniel declared, "I saw in my vision by night, and behold, the four winds of heaven were stirring up the great sea. And four great beasts came up out of the sea, different from one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With chapter 7 the book changes. Stories give way to visions in Daniel's own voice, arranged by theme rather than strict date. This vision came in the first year of Belshazzar, years before Babylon fell in chapter 5.

This chapter is the hinge of the whole book. It is still written in Aramaic (see the note at 2:4), so it belongs with chapters 2-6. But it looks forward to chapters 8-12.

In the Bible the sea often pictures the restless, chaotic world of nations opposed to God. Isaiah wrote of the roar of nations; they roar like the roaring of mighty waters (Isa 17:12), and the wicked are like the tossing sea; for it cannot be quiet (Isa 57:20). The four winds of heaven suggest that the storm comes from every direction, and that heaven is the one stirring it. Even the turmoil of world history is under God's hand.

Four beasts rise from the storm. They are the four kingdoms of chapter 2's statue, now seen as they really are: a pagan king saw a shining statue, God's prophet sees devouring beasts. What the world admires, heaven sees as monstrous.
verseByVerse.note: The first year of Belshazzar was about 553 BC, before chapter 5.

verseByVerse.quote: The first was like a lion and had eagles' wings. Then as I looked its wings were plucked off, and it was lifted up from the ground and made to stand on two feet like a man, and the mind of a man was given to it. And behold, another beast, a second one, like a bear. It was raised up on one side. It had three ribs in its mouth between its teeth; and it was told, 'Arise, devour much flesh.' After this I looked, and behold, another, like a leopard, with four wings of a bird on its back. And the beast had four heads, and dominion was given to it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first beast is Babylon, the head of gold. The lion was the king of beasts, and the eagle the king of birds, a fitting image for Nebuchadnezzar's mighty and swift empire. Jeremiah pictured Babylon's attack as a lion leaving its thicket (Jer 4:7), and Ezekiel pictured the king of Babylon as a great eagle (Ezek 17:3, 12).

Then something strange happens. The wings are torn off, and the beast stands up like a man and receives the mind of a man. This probably recalls chapter 4, where Nebuchadnezzar lost his human mind, lived like a beast and then had his reason restored.

The second beast matches the silver of chapter 2: the empire of the Medes and Persians. The bear is raised up on one side, probably because the empire had two partners and one, Persia, became much stronger than the other. Chapter 8 pictures the same empire as a ram with two horns, one higher than the other (8:3, 20). The three ribs in its mouth may represent the major conquests it had swallowed, though we cannot be sure which ones. And it is told to devour. Even the beasts act only when permitted.

The third beast matches the bronze: Greece. The leopard is fast, and with four wings it is faster still. That fits Alexander the Great, who in about ten years built an empire stretching from Greece to the borders of India. The four heads fit what happened after his early death, when his empire was divided into four main kingdoms ruled by his generals. Chapter 8 describes exactly that: when the great horn was broken, four kingdoms shall arise from his nation, but not with his power (8:22).

Again, dominion was given to it. Every empire receives its power from the Most High.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I saw in the night visions, and behold, a fourth beast, terrifying and dreadful and exceedingly strong. It had great iron teeth; it devoured and broke in pieces and stamped what was left with its feet. It was different from all the beasts that were before it, and it had ten horns. I considered the horns, and behold, there came up among them another horn, a little one, before which three of the first horns were plucked up by the roots. And behold, in this horn were eyes like the eyes of a man, and a mouth speaking great things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fourth beast is so terrible that Daniel cannot compare it to any known animal. Its iron teeth link it to the legs of iron in chapter 2. As set out at 2:39-40, the traditional understanding, followed here, sees this as Rome, which crushed every power in its path. (Those who read the four kingdoms as Babylon, Media, Persia and Greece see this beast as Greece.)

The beast has ten horns. In the Bible a horn is a symbol of strength, and especially of a king's power. The angel will explain that the ten horns are ten kings (v. 24).

Daniel's attention fixes on a little horn that grows among the others and uproots three of them. It has eyes like the eyes of a man, suggesting intelligence and watchfulness, and a mouth speaking great things, boastful words against God (v. 25).

Who is this little horn? Christians have held three main views. Many believe it is a final ruler who will oppose God and persecute his people at the end of history, the one Paul calls the man of lawlessness who exalts himself against every so-called god or object of worship (2 Thess 2:3-4), and whom Revelation pictures as a beast with a mouth uttering haughty and blasphemous words (Rev 13:5). Others, who take the fourth kingdom as Greece, identify the little horn with Antiochus IV, a Greek king who persecuted the Jews in the second century BC. Their reason is weighty: chapter 8 describes him with very similar marks, a boastful horn that attacks God's people and stops their worship, and he did try to abolish the Jewish festivals and law (v. 25). Even many who see a final enemy here grant that Antiochus was a preview of him. Many Protestants in the centuries after the Reformation saw the horn as the papacy. The first view is the one most widely held today among Reformed and other evangelical interpreters. It also fits the chapter's own claim that the horn's defeat is followed directly by the final judgment and the everlasting kingdom (vv. 26-27). John adds a helpful balance: as you have heard that antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have come (1 John 2:18). The final enemy will be foreshadowed by many proud rulers before him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–14 — The Ancient of Days and the Son of Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Thrones are placed and the Ancient of Days took his seat, dazzling white and surrounded by fire and countless servants; the court sat in judgment, and the books were opened (vv. 9-10). The beast is destroyed and the others lose their dominion (vv. 11-12). Then with the clouds of heaven there came one like a son of man, who receives from the Ancient of Days an everlasting dominion over all peoples (vv. 13-14).
verseByVerse.theology: God sits in judgment over the beasts and gives the everlasting kingdom to the Son of Man, Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "As I looked, thrones were placed, and the Ancient of Days took his seat; his clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool; his throne was fiery flames; its wheels were burning fire. A stream of fire issued and came out from before him; a thousand thousands served him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him; the court sat in judgment, and the books were opened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Suddenly the scene moves from the stormy sea to heaven's courtroom. While the little horn is still boasting on earth, thrones were placed in heaven, and a judge takes his seat.

He is called the Ancient of Days, a title found only in this chapter. It means the one who is old beyond all time, the eternal God. The beasts are new arrivals in history, rising and falling. He was there before them all. His white clothing speaks of purity and his white hair of wisdom and eternal age. His throne is fiery flames, with wheels of fire, like the living throne-chariot Ezekiel saw by the Chebar canal (Ezek 1). Fire speaks of holiness and judgment.

Then, in the New Testament, something astonishing happens. When John sees the risen Jesus, he describes him with the words of this verse: The hairs of his head were white, like white wool, like snow (Rev 1:14). The features of the Ancient of Days belong to Christ. He shares the eternal glory of God.

A river of fire flows from the throne, and countless heavenly servants surround it, ten thousand times ten thousand, more than can be counted. The books are the records of what the beasts have done. Nothing has been forgotten. Revelation uses the same picture: books were opened... And the dead were judged by what was written in the books, according to what they had done (Rev 20:12).

This is deeply comforting for God's persecuted people. Tyrants may seem to act without consequences. But every word, every cruelty and every martyr is recorded, and the court will sit.

verseByVerse.quote: "I looked then because of the sound of the great words that the horn was speaking. And as I looked, the beast was killed, and its body destroyed and given over to be burned with fire. As for the rest of the beasts, their dominion was taken away, but their lives were prolonged for a season and a time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Daniel's eyes are drawn back to earth by the noise of the horn's boasting. With no battle described, the verdict is carried out. The beast was killed. All its loud words cannot save it. He who sits in the heavens laughs; the Lord holds them in derision (Ps 2:4).

The earlier beasts are treated differently. Their power to rule is taken away, but they are not destroyed at once. Conquered empires lived on for a while inside the next. The fourth beast, however, will be completely destroyed at the final judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: "I saw in the night visions, and behold, with the clouds of heaven there came one like a son of man, and he came to the Ancient of Days and was presented before him. And to him was given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him; his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom one that shall not be destroyed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the high point of the chapter and one of the most important verses in the Bible. After four beasts comes one like a son of man, which means one who looks like a human being. The contrast is intentional. The kingdoms of the world are beastly. God's kingdom will be ruled by one who is truly human, as God intended humanity to rule from the beginning (Gen 1:26-28).

But he is more than a man. He comes with the clouds of heaven. In the Old Testament, riding on the clouds is a picture used of God himself: he makes the clouds his chariot (Ps 104:3). This figure is human, yet he travels as God travels. And he is brought into the very presence of the Ancient of Days.

Jesus called himself the Son of Man more than any other title, and he drew it above all from this verse. At his trial, when the high priest demanded, Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?, Jesus answered: I am, and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven (Mark 14:61-62). The high priest tore his clothes and charged him with blasphemy. He understood exactly what Jesus was claiming: to be the divine-human King of Daniel 7. The prisoner standing bound before him was the one before whom every throne on earth will one day stand.

The direction of travel matters. The son of man comes to the Ancient of Days, from earth to heaven's throne. Many interpreters see this fulfilled first in Christ's ascension, when a cloud took him out of their sight (Acts 1:9) and he was enthroned in heaven. Stephen, as he was dying, saw the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God (Acts 7:56). And the same Jesus will come again with the clouds to earth: Behold, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him (Rev 1:7). His kingdom has been received, and it will be revealed.

Everything the beasts grasped at is now given to him: dominion and glory and a kingdom. Nebuchadnezzar demanded that peoples, nations, and languages bow to his image (3:4). Now all peoples, nations, and languages will serve the Son of Man. And his kingdom, unlike every beastly empire, shall not pass away.

After his resurrection, Jesus spoke as the one who had received this kingdom: All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me (Matt 28:18). That is why the church goes to all nations with the gospel. The kingdom of the Son of Man is gathering its people from every language on earth.

How Jewish readers take it. Older Jewish tradition often read the one like a son of man as the Messiah: the Talmud (Sanhedrin 98a) sets this verse beside Zechariah 9:9, saying the Messiah comes with the clouds if Israel is worthy and lowly on a donkey if not, and Rashi names him the King Messiah. Many Jewish readers today, noting verses 18 and 27, take him as a figure for faithful Israel, the saints who receive the kingdom. Both readings honour something in the chapter. This commentary sees in him the Messiah who also represents his people, as Jesus claimed at his trial (Mark 14:62).
verseByVerse.note: At his trial Jesus joined this verse to Psalm 110:1, “seated at the right hand” (Mark 14:62).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–22 — The Saints Shall Receive the Kingdom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The four beasts are four kings, but the saints will receive the kingdom, even after the horn prevails over them for a time (vv. 15-22).
verseByVerse.theology: The people of God may be overpowered for a time, but the kingdom is finally theirs.

verseByVerse.quote: "As for me, Daniel, my spirit within me was anxious, and the visions of my head alarmed me. I approached one of those who stood there and asked him the truth concerning all this. So he told me and made known to me the interpretation of the things. 'These four great beasts are four kings who shall arise out of the earth. But the saints of the Most High shall receive the kingdom and possess the kingdom forever, forever and ever.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Daniel was deeply disturbed. The ESV notes that within me is literally "within its sheath", a picture of the body as the sheath that holds the spirit, like a sword. Seeing the future clearly did not make Daniel proud or excited. It made him tremble. Prophecy is not given to satisfy curiosity but to prepare God's people.

Daniel does what every reader of prophecy should do. He asks for the true meaning, and he receives it from heaven. We too need God's own interpretation, and we have it, in the rest of Scripture.

The beasts came up from the sea (v. 3). Here they arise out of the earth. Both images make the same point: these kingdoms have a purely earthly origin, in contrast to the son of man who comes with the clouds of heaven. The kings stand for their kingdoms (v. 23).

The saints are God's holy people, those set apart to belong to him. The kingdom given to the son of man in verse 14 is also given to his people. The King shares his reign with those who belong to him.

Some readers have taken this to mean that the son of man is simply a symbol for the saints. But the New Testament shows how the two belong together. Jesus is the King, and his people reign with him. The one who conquers, I will grant him to sit with me on my throne, as I also conquered and sat down with my Father on his throne (Rev 3:21). If we endure, we will also reign with him (2 Tim 2:12). And Jesus told his small, weak band of followers: Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom (Luke 12:32).

verseByVerse.quote: "Then I desired to know the truth about the fourth beast, which was different from all the rest, exceedingly terrifying, with its teeth of iron and claws of bronze, and which devoured and broke in pieces and stamped what was left with its feet, and about the ten horns that were on its head, and the other horn that came up and before which three of them fell, the horn that had eyes and a mouth that spoke great things, and that seemed greater than its companions. As I looked, this horn made war with the saints and prevailed over them, until the Ancient of Days came, and judgment was given for the saints of the Most High, and the time came when the saints possessed the kingdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Daniel is most troubled by the fourth beast and its little horn, just as we would expect.

Here is something the first description did not mention. The horn made war with the saints and prevailed over them. God's people will not always win in this world. For a time they will be defeated, persecuted and killed. Revelation says the same of the beast: it was allowed to make war on the saints and to conquer them (Rev 13:7). Christians should not be shocked when faithfulness leads to suffering. It was foretold.

But the key word is until. The horn's victory has an end date. Until the Ancient of Days came. Then judgment was given for the saints. The court rules in favour of the persecuted. The kingdom that the horn tried to seize is handed to the people it oppressed. Paul reminds believers of their future: do you not know that the saints will judge the world? (1 Cor 6:2).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–28 — Time, Times, and Half a Time
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The angel explains the fourth kingdom and the horn that will wear out the saints for a time, times, and half a time, until the court sits and the kingdom is given to the saints (vv. 23-28).
verseByVerse.theology: The persecution of God's people is real but limited, and God's judgment and kingdom are certain.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus he said: 'As for the fourth beast, there shall be a fourth kingdom on earth, which shall be different from all the kingdoms, and it shall devour the whole earth, and trample it down, and break it to pieces. As for the ten horns, out of this kingdom ten kings shall arise, and another shall arise after them; he shall be different from the former ones, and shall put down three kings. He shall speak words against the Most High, and shall wear out the saints of the Most High, and shall think to change the times and the law; and they shall be given into his hand for a time, times, and half a time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some take the ten as literal rulers of a final world order. Others take ten as a round number for the full set of powers that come from the fourth kingdom. Revelation also speaks of ten horns as ten kings who have not yet received royal power, ruling together with the beast (Rev 17:12).

Here are the marks of this final enemy of God. He will speak words against the Most High, exalting himself against God. He will wear out the saints, not always by a single violent blow, but by constant, grinding pressure. And he will think to change the times and the law, trying to overturn God's order: the sacred calendar, the worship of God and the moral law itself. Every age has seen rulers who tried to redefine what is good, erase the memory of God from public life and wear down believers until they give up.

But his power is given. They shall be given into his hand, for a set period. A time, times, and half a time most likely means one year, two years and half a year: three and a half. Some Christians, especially dispensationalists, take this as a literal period of three and a half years at the very end of history. Many others, including many in the Reformed tradition, take it as a symbolic number for a limited period of persecution. Three and a half is half of seven, the number of completeness. The enemy's time is broken off halfway. This commentary takes the symbolic reading, in keeping with its amillennial view, while honouring those who differ. Revelation counts the same period as a time, times and half a time (Rev 12:14), forty-two months and 1,260 days (Rev 11:2–3; 12:6), and applies it to the church's whole time of witness in the world. Either way, the comfort is the same. The persecution is real, but it is measured, limited and controlled by God.
verseByVerse.note: “A time, times, and half a time” makes three and a half, half of seven: a limited period of persecution, cut short by God.

verseByVerse.quote: But the court shall sit in judgment, and his dominion shall be taken away, to be consumed and destroyed to the end. And the kingdom and the dominion and the greatness of the kingdoms under the whole heaven shall be given to the people of the saints of the Most High; his kingdom shall be an everlasting kingdom, and all dominions shall serve and obey him.' "Here is the end of the matter. As for me, Daniel, my thoughts greatly alarmed me, and my color changed, but I kept the matter in my heart."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel returns, as the vision did, to the court. But the court shall sit. However loud the horn becomes, however long the saints are worn down, a day of judgment is coming, and his dominion will be destroyed to the end. He will never rise again.

All the greatness of the kingdoms under the whole heaven, everything the beasts ever possessed, will be given to God's people. The ESV notes that the second half of the verse could also be read "their kingdom shall be an everlasting kingdom, and all dominions shall serve and obey them". Both readings are true together. The kingdom belongs to God and his King, and he shares it with his people. And they will reign forever and ever (Rev 22:5).

Daniel does not come away from the vision with a chart of dates. He comes away shaken, pale and thoughtful. And he kept the matter in my heart, treasuring it and pondering it, as Mary would do with the words spoken about her Son: Mary treasured up all these things, pondering them in her heart (Luke 2:19).

That is the right response to biblical prophecy. Its purpose is not to feed speculation about which world leader is the little horn. Its purpose is to steady God's people. The beasts are real, and they may prevail for a while. But the court is already seated, the Son of Man has already received the kingdom, and the saints will possess it forever. When the news seems full of beasts, Christians can lift their eyes to the throne.

7.title: One Like a Son of Man
7.overview: Daniel 7 is the hinge of the book. Daniel sees four beasts rise from a stormy sea, the last and most terrible with a boastful little horn (vv. 1-8). Then heaven's court sits, the Ancient of Days takes his throne, and one like a son of man comes with the clouds to receive an everlasting kingdom (vv. 9-14). An angel explains that the saints of the Most High will share that kingdom, though the horn will make war on them for a limited time (vv. 15-28). The same four kingdoms as the statue of chapter 2 are seen here as heaven sees them, and the Son of Man in their midst is the one Jesus claimed to be.
7.theology:
God rules over the turmoil of history; the empires of the world, however glorious they appear, are beastly in God's sight and hold power only as it is given to them (vv. 2-7).

The Ancient of Days is the eternal Judge who records every deed; the court will sit and the proud will be destroyed (vv. 9-12, 26; Ps 2:4; Rev 20:12).

The one like a son of man, coming with the clouds and receiving an everlasting kingdom, is Jesus Christ, who shares the glory of God, has received all authority and will come again (vv. 13-14; Mark 14:61-62; Acts 1:9; 7:56; Matt 28:18; Rev 1:7, 13-14).

The saints share the kingdom of their King and will reign with him forever (vv. 18, 22, 27; Luke 12:32; Rev 3:21; 22:5; 2 Tim 2:12; 1 Cor 6:2).

A final enemy will blaspheme God and persecute his people, foreshadowed by many antichrists, but his time is limited and his defeat certain (vv. 8, 21, 24-26; 2 Thess 2:3-4; 1 John 2:18; Rev 13:5-7).

Prophecy is given not to feed speculation but to steady God's people in suffering (vv. 15, 28).
7.examples: When the news is full of beasts, war, tyranny and believers worn down by grinding pressure, Daniel 7 tells us where to look. The court is seated, the books are open, and the Son of Man already holds the kingdom. A Christian imprisoned for the faith, or simply mocked at work, can know that the horn's time is measured and that the kingdom is promised to the saints.
