verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Vision at the Ulai
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Daniel sees a two-horned ram shattered by a swift goat, and a little horn from the goat's line that defiles the sanctuary For 2,300 evenings and mornings (vv. 1-14).
verseByVerse.theology: Empires rise and fall at God's word, and even the desecration of his sanctuary has a limit he has fixed.

verseByVerse.quote: In the third year of the reign of King Belshazzar a vision appeared to me, Daniel, after that which appeared to me at the first. And I saw in the vision; and when I saw, I was in Susa the citadel, which is in the province of Elam. And I saw in the vision, and I was at the Ulai canal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This vision came two years after the vision of chapter 7, still before the fall of Babylon. From here the book is in Hebrew again, and its focus narrows to God's own people and his sanctuary.

Daniel was taken in the vision to Susa, some two hundred miles east of Babylon. Susa would soon become a Persian capital. Esther lived there, in Susa, the citadel (Esth 1:2), and Nehemiah served the Persian king there (Neh 1:1). God set the scene of the vision in the future centre of the next world power.
verseByVerse.note: Susa lay in Elam, in what is now south-western Iran.

verseByVerse.quote: I raised my eyes and saw, and behold, a ram standing on the bank of the canal. It had two horns, and both horns were high, but one was higher than the other, and the higher one came up last. I saw the ram charging westward and northward and southward. No beast could stand before him, and there was no one who could rescue from his power. He did as he pleased and became great.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We do not have to guess what the ram means. Gabriel says it plainly: these are the kings of Media and Persia (v. 20). The two horns are the two peoples united in one empire. The Medes were the stronger partner at first, but Persia came up last and grew higher, until under Cyrus it dominated the partnership. This matches the bear raised up on one side in 7:5.

For two centuries no one could stop Persia. He did as he pleased and became great. That is the recurring sin of empires in Daniel: power that answers to no one. But the phrase is also a warning. In this book, those who do as they please are always about to meet the God who does according to his will (4:35).
verseByVerse.note: The ram is Media-Persia (v. 20).

verseByVerse.quote: As I was considering, behold, a male goat came from the west across the face of the whole earth, without touching the ground. And the goat had a conspicuous horn between his eyes. He came to the ram with the two horns, which I had seen standing on the bank of the canal, and he ran at him in his powerful wrath. I saw him come close to the ram, and he was enraged against him and struck the ram and broke his two horns. And the ram had no power to stand before him, but he cast him down to the ground and trampled on him. And there was no one who could rescue the ram from his power. Then the goat became exceedingly great, but when he was strong, the great horn was broken, and instead of it there came up four conspicuous horns toward the four winds of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A goat charges in from the west so fast that its feet do not seem to touch the ground. Gabriel explains: the goat is the king of Greece. And the great horn between his eyes is the first king (v. 21). (The ESV notes it may be "the shaggy goat".) Alexander the Great crossed from Greece into Asia in 334 BC, and within about three years he had broken the power of the Persian empire.

The words of verse 4 are turned back on the ram. Once there was no one who could rescue from his power. Now there was no one who could rescue the ram.

When he was strong, the great horn was broken. At the very height of his power, in 323 BC, Alexander died suddenly in Babylon, only about thirty-two years old. He had conquered the known world and could not conquer death. His empire was eventually divided among his generals into four main kingdoms, toward the four winds of heaven, just as the leopard of chapter 7 had four heads. Pride goes before destruction (Prov 16:18).
verseByVerse.note: The goat is Greece; its great horn, Alexander the Great, who died young in 323 BC and whose empire split four ways.

verseByVerse.quote: Out of one of them came a little horn, which grew exceedingly great toward the south, toward the east, and toward the glorious land. It grew great, even to the host of heaven. And some of the host and some of the stars it threw down to the ground and trampled on them. It became great, even as great as the Prince of the host. And the regular burnt offering was taken away from him, and the place of his sanctuary was overthrown. And a host will be given over to it together with the regular burnt offering because of transgression, and it will throw truth to the ground, and it will act and prosper.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the vision narrows to one ruler. A little horn grows out of one of the four Greek kingdoms. It is not the horn of chapter 7, which came from the fourth beast; this one comes from Greece.

There is wide agreement about who this little horn is: Antiochus IV, a king of the Seleucid dynasty, which ruled Syria and the lands to the east. He reigned from 175 to 164 BC and called himself Epiphanes, meaning "God made manifest". He campaigned toward the south (Egypt), toward the east (Persia) and toward the glorious land, the land of Israel, which Daniel loved.

The horn's pride reaches toward heaven itself. The host of heaven and the stars are probably a picture of God's people, who are elsewhere in Daniel compared to stars (12:3), and of the heavenly armies who stand behind them. The ESV notes that it may read "the host, that is, some of the stars", making the host and the stars one and the same. Antiochus attacked the faithful Jews as if he were attacking heaven, and in a sense he was. To persecute God's people is to make war on God.

The Prince of the host is God himself, the commander of heaven's armies. The horn sets itself up as God's equal. And it strikes at the heart of Israel's worship. The regular burnt offering was the lamb offered every morning and evening in the temple (Exod 29:38-42). In 167 BC Antiochus stopped these sacrifices, set up pagan worship in God's temple and forbade the Jews on pain of death to keep the Sabbath, circumcise their sons or own the Scriptures. The Jewish history book known as 1 Maccabees records these horrors.

Two things stand out. First, all this happens because of transgression. The ESV notes it may mean "in an act of rebellion". Either Israel's own sin opened the door to this judgment, or the horn's rebellion is in view. In fact both were true: many Jews of that time were eagerly abandoning God's law for Greek ways. Second, the horn will throw truth to the ground. Tyranny always attacks truth, because God's truth exposes its lies. And for a time it will act and prosper. God's people must be ready for evil to succeed for a season.
verseByVerse.note: The little horn is usually identified as Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who desecrated the temple in 167 BC.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I heard a holy one speaking, and another holy one said to the one who spoke, "For how long is the vision concerning the regular burnt offering, the transgression that makes desolate, and the giving over of the sanctuary and host to be trampled underfoot?" And he said to me, "For 2,300 evenings and mornings. Then the sanctuary shall be restored to its rightful state."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even angels ask the question God's suffering people ask: For how long? It is the cry of the psalms: How long, O God, is the foe to scoff? (Ps 74:10). It is the cry of the martyrs in Revelation: how long before you will judge and avenge our blood (Rev 6:10)?

The phrase the transgression that makes desolate introduces an idea that will return in 9:27, 11:31 and 12:11: an outrage against God so terrible that it leaves his sanctuary desolate. Jesus himself would take up this language when he warned of the abomination of desolation spoken of by the prophet Daniel (Matt 24:15).

The answer is a number, and the number means there is a limit. God has counted the days of the desecration.

What does 2,300 evenings and mornings mean? There are two main readings. Some take it as 2,300 days, a little over six years, perhaps counting from the first attacks on the faithful to the end of Antiochus's persecution. Others note that the temple had an evening and a morning offering each day, so 2,300 offerings would be 1,150 days, a little over three years. That is close to the time between the desecration of the temple in 167 BC and its cleansing and rededication by faithful Jews in December 164 BC, which was exactly three years by the Jewish calendar (1 Maccabees 1:54; 4:52). The second reading fits well, since the evening and morning offerings had just been named as taken away (v. 11), though 1,150 days runs about two months beyond three years, and no reading fits every date exactly. Either way, God set a date, and the sanctuary was restored.

The Jews celebrated that rededication every year afterward with the Feast of Dedication, known today as Hanukkah. The Gospel of John tells us that Jesus was in the temple at that very feast: At that time the Feast of Dedication took place at Jerusalem. It was winter, and Jesus was walking in the temple (John 10:22-23). There, while the people remembered the cleansing of the temple, Jesus spoke of himself as the one whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world (John 10:36). The true temple, the place where God dwells with man, was walking among them. He was speaking about the temple of his body (John 2:21).

Seventh-day Adventists have read the 2,300 days as 2,300 years, ending in 1844, when, they teach, Christ began a work of judgment in the heavenly sanctuary. But the text speaks of evenings and mornings, not years; the vision is for the time of the end of the Greek kingdom (vv. 17, 21–23), and the sanctuary here is the temple Antiochus defiled. And Hebrews teaches that Christ entered the heavenly holy places once for all at his ascension (Heb 9:12, 24), not in 1844.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gabriel explains the vision: the ram is Media and Persia, the goat is Greece, and a bold king will rise against the Prince of princes and he shall be broken—but by no human hand (vv. 15-27).
verseByVerse.theology: God tells his people in advance what they will suffer, so that when it comes they will know he still rules.

verseByVerse.quote: When I, Daniel, had seen the vision, I sought to understand it. And behold, there stood before me one having the appearance of a man. And I heard a man's voice between the banks of the Ulai, and it called, "Gabriel, make this man understand the vision." So he came near where I stood. And when he came, I was frightened and fell on my face. But he said to me, "Understand, O son of man, that the vision is for the time of the end." And when he had spoken to me, I fell into a deep sleep with my face to the ground. But he touched me and made me stand up. He said, "Behold, I will make known to you what shall be at the latter end of the indignation, for it refers to the appointed time of the end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the first time an angel is named in the Bible. Gabriel is sent to explain the vision. Five centuries later he appears to Zechariah and Mary. I am Gabriel. I stand in the presence of God (Luke 1:19). The same messenger who explained the rise and fall of empires to Daniel announced the birth of the King whose kingdom has no end (Luke 1:26-33).

Who gives Gabriel the order? A man's voice from between the banks of the Ulai. The book does not say who it is, but he has authority to command Gabriel. Many have connected him with the man clothed in linen who stands above the waters of the stream in 12:6-7.

Gabriel calls Daniel son of man, the same way God addressed Ezekiel (Ezek 2:1). Here it simply means "mortal man", a reminder of how small Daniel is before the messengers of God.

What is the time of the end? In this chapter the explanation focuses on the end of the indignation, the period of God's anger against his people's sin, which came to its climax under Antiochus. But the vision also looks beyond him. Antiochus is a preview of a greater enemy who will arise at the final end of history. The persecutor of chapter 8 and the horn of chapter 7 share the same marks: pride, blasphemy and war on God's people and worship. What happened under Antiochus is a pattern of what the church must expect before Christ returns.

And the end is appointed: God has fixed it.
verseByVerse.note: Only two angels are named in the Old Testament, Gabriel and Michael (10:13), both in Daniel.

verseByVerse.quote: As for the ram that you saw with the two horns, these are the kings of Media and Persia. And the goat is the king of Greece. And the great horn between his eyes is the first king. As for the horn that was broken, in place of which four others arose, four kingdoms shall arise from his nation, but not with his power.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Few prophecies in the Bible are so specific. Gabriel names the empires: Media and Persia, then Greece. Yet the vision describes nearly four centuries of history before they happened. This precision is the main reason many scholars think the book was written after the events, about 165 BC. This commentary holds that God, who knows the end from the beginning, gave Daniel these things in advance, while granting that the date of the book is debated (see the Introduction).

These verses also bear on chapters 2 and 7. Here Media and Persia are one animal, and Greece comes next, which is a main reason this commentary reads the silver kingdom and the bear as Medo-Persia, the bronze and the leopard as Greece, and the fourth kingdom as Rome (see 2:39-40).

verseByVerse.quote: And at the latter end of their kingdom, when the transgressors have reached their limit, a king of bold face, one who understands riddles, shall arise. His power shall be great— but not by his own power; and he shall cause fearful destruction and shall succeed in what he does, and destroy mighty men and the people who are the saints. By his cunning he shall make deceit prosper under his hand, and in his own mind he shall become great. Without warning he shall destroy many. And he shall even rise up against the Prince of princes, and he shall be broken—but by no human hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the transgressors have reached their limit. God allows sin to run its course until the measure is full, and then he acts. The king of bold face is shameless and hard. He understands riddles, meaning he is clever at scheming and double-dealing. Antiochus was famous for his cunning.

But not by his own power. However frightening he becomes, his strength is given to him. He is a tool in a hand larger than his own. He will destroy... the people who are the saints. Daniel is not promised that God's people will be spared, only that God is still in control.

His weapons are cunning and deceit. He attacks without warning. And in his own mind he shall become great, the same inward pride that brought down Nebuchadnezzar. Finally he goes too far and rises against the Prince of princes, God himself.

Then comes his end: he shall be broken—but by no human hand. These are the words used of the stone in 2:34. Antiochus was not killed in battle. He died of a sudden illness while campaigning in the east in 164 BC. God himself removed him.

The Prince of princes has one final answer to every tyrant. They will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings (Rev 17:14). The rulers of the earth once took counsel together against God's Anointed, Jesus, and crucified him. But they did only whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place (Acts 4:28), and God raised him from the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: The vision of the evenings and the mornings that has been told is true, but seal up the vision, for it refers to many days from now." And I, Daniel, was overcome and lay sick for some days. Then I rose and went about the king's business, but I was appalled by the vision and did not understand it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seal up the vision does not mean hide it. It means preserve it safely, like a legal document sealed for the future. The events were many days from now, nearly four hundred years away. When they came, the faithful Jews who suffered under Antiochus would be able to open Daniel and know that God had foreseen every step of their suffering and had set its limit. For whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction, that through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope (Rom 15:4).

The vision made Daniel physically ill. He had seen the future suffering of his people and the desecration of God's sanctuary, and it crushed him.

And yet, when he recovered, I rose and went about the king's business. Knowing the future did not make him quit and wait for the end. Christians, too, serve faithfully in the present, not by straining to master the timeline, but because the God who holds the future holds them.

Daniel admits that he did not understand it. Even the prophet did not grasp everything he saw. Peter says that the prophets searched and inquired carefully about the things they foretold, and that they were serving not themselves but you (1 Pet 1:10, 12). We live on the far side of these events. We can see how they came true, and we can see in them the pattern of the final conflict before Christ returns. Most of all, we know the Prince against whom every little horn rises, and we know that he has already won.

8.title: The Ram and the Goat
8.overview: Two years after chapter 7, Daniel sees a ram with two horns trampled by a swift goat, whose great horn is broken and replaced by four (vv. 1-8). From one of them grows a little horn that attacks God's people, stops the daily offerings and defiles the sanctuary, but only for a set time (vv. 9-14). Gabriel names the ram as Media and Persia and the goat as Greece, and he describes a bold king who will rise against the Prince of princes and be broken by no human hand (vv. 15-27). The chapter narrows the book's focus to God's own people and his sanctuary in the dark years under the Greek king Antiochus IV, and it shows that even that suffering had a limit God had fixed.
8.theology:
God knows and announces the rise and fall of empires long before they happen (vv. 3-8, 20-22; Rom 15:4).

Pride and unchecked power end in ruin; the greatest conquerors are broken at God's word (vv. 4, 7-8, 25; Prov 16:18).

To attack God's people and worship is to make war on God, and God permits such evil only for a fixed and limited time (vv. 10-14, 24; Ps 74:10; Rev 6:10).

The desecrations of history, like Antiochus's, foreshadow the final enemy of God and his people (vv. 17, 19; Matt 24:15).

The restored sanctuary points to Christ, the true temple consecrated by the Father, whose single sacrifice fulfils the regular offerings (vv. 11-14; John 2:19-21; 10:22, 36; Heb 10:11-12).

Every enemy who rises against the Prince of princes is broken by God, and Christ the Lamb conquers (v. 25; Rev 17:14; Acts 4:26-28).

Prophecy is given to steady God's people, and they serve faithfully in the present while trusting God with what they do not understand (v. 27; 1 Pet 1:10-12).
8.examples: Daniel 8 was written for believers who would one day watch their faith outlawed and their worship stopped. When they suffered under Antiochus, they could open this chapter and see that God had foreseen every step and set its end. Christians who face hostile rulers now can read it the same way, and then, like Daniel, get up and go back to their work.

And for sixty-two weeks it shall be built again with squares and moat, but in a troubled time.<sup>26</sup>And after the sixty-two weeks, an anointed one shall be cut off and shall have nothing. verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the first year of Darius, Daniel perceived in the books the number of years that Jeremiah had said must pass before the end of Jerusalem's desolations: seventy years (vv. 1-2).
verseByVerse.theology: God's promises in Scripture move his people to pray.

verseByVerse.quote: In the first year of Darius the son of Ahasuerus, by descent a Mede, who was made king over the realm of the Chaldeans— in the first year of his reign, I, Daniel, perceived in the books the number of years that, according to the word of the LORD to Jeremiah the prophet, must pass before the end of the desolations of Jerusalem, namely, seventy years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The date is 539 or 538 BC. Babylon has just fallen, as chapter 5 described. Daniel is now an old man, probably over eighty. He has lived through the whole of Babylon's empire and has seen it collapse in a single night. (Who Darius the Mede was is debated: perhaps another title for Cyrus, perhaps the governor Cyrus set over Babylon; see 5:31.)

The books were the Scriptures available to him, including Jeremiah, his older contemporary. Jeremiah had said, When seventy years are completed for Babylon, I will visit you, and I will fulfill to you my promise and bring you back to this place (Jer 29:10). Daniel had been taken captive in 605 BC. Now Babylon had fallen. He did the arithmetic. The seventy years were almost over.

Chronicles explains why the exile lasted seventy years. The land had to make up for the Sabbath years Israel had failed to keep: All the days that it lay desolate it kept Sabbath, to fulfill seventy years (2 Chr 36:21). That detail will matter when we come to the seventy "weeks" at the end of the chapter.

Finding the promise about to be fulfilled, Daniel did not sit back and wait. He prayed. God's sovereign promises never make prayer unnecessary. They make it confident. Jeremiah's own prophecy said so: Then you will call upon me and come and pray to me, and I will hear you (Jer 29:12). The Bible's promises are meant to be turned into prayers, and the Spirit himself helps believers to pray them (Rom 8:26).
verseByVerse.note: Daniel reads Jeremiah’s prophecy of seventy years of exile.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Daniel confesses Israel's sin and God's justice in the curses of the Law (vv. 3-14), then pleads for the city and sanctuary on one ground only: God's great mercy (vv. 15-19).
verseByVerse.theology: True prayer confesses sin honestly and pleads only God's mercy and the honor of his name.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I turned my face to the Lord God, seeking him by prayer and pleas for mercy with fasting and sackcloth and ashes. I prayed to the LORD my God and made confession, saying, "O Lord, the great and awesome God, who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who love him and keep his commandments, we have sinned and done wrong and acted wickedly and rebelled, turning aside from your commandments and rules. We have not listened to your servants the prophets, who spoke in your name to our kings, our princes, and our fathers, and to all the people of the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fasting, rough sackcloth and ashes on the head were signs of mourning and humility. Daniel's whole body joined in his prayer, expressing sorrow over sin.

Daniel begins with God, not with his own needs. God is great and awesome, and he keeps covenant and steadfast love. Before Daniel speaks of Israel's unfaithfulness, he remembers God's faithfulness. That is where every prayer of confession must begin, or confession turns into despair.

The confession piles up words for sin and makes no excuses. And the pronoun is we. Daniel is the most faithful man in the book. Enemies searched his life and found no fault (6:4). Yet he does not pray "they have sinned". He stands with his people and confesses their sin as his own. Ezra and Nehemiah later prayed the same way (Ezra 9:6; Neh 1:6). God's law had promised that if his exiled people would confess their iniquity and the iniquity of their fathers, he would remember my covenant (Lev 26:40, 42). Daniel is doing exactly what God asked.

In this Daniel points us to Christ, who went much further. Daniel identified with sinners and confessed sins he shared. Jesus, who had no sin at all, took the sins of his people upon himself. He bore the sin of many, and makes intercession for the transgressors (Isa 53:12).

At the root of Israel's disaster was a refusal to listen. God had spoken again and again through the prophets, from kings to ordinary people, and they would not hear. That is still the root of spiritual ruin: not a lack of God's word, but a refusal to listen to it.

verseByVerse.quote: To you, O Lord, belongs righteousness, but to us open shame, as at this day, to the men of Judah, to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and to all Israel, those who are near and those who are far away, in all the lands to which you have driven them, because of the treachery that they have committed against you. To us, O LORD, belongs open shame, to our kings, to our princes, and to our fathers, because we have sinned against you. To the Lord our God belong mercy and forgiveness, for we have rebelled against him and have not obeyed the voice of the LORD our God by walking in his laws, which he set before us by his servants the prophets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Daniel sets two things side by side. To you... belongs righteousness. God was right to send the exile. But to us open shame. Israel had no complaint to make. The scattered people, near and far away, were living proof that God had kept his word.

This is the heart of genuine repentance. It does not say, "God, why did you do this to me?" It says, "God, you are just, and the fault is mine." The tax collector in Jesus' parable prayed only, God, be merciful to me, a sinner! (Luke 18:13), and he went home justified.

Here is the turn in the prayer. God has righteousness, and he also has mercy and forgiveness. Israel has only shame, and yet Daniel dares to hope, because mercy belongs to God. He even gives the reason: for we have rebelled. He does not say God should forgive because Israel deserves it. He appeals to mercy precisely because they do not deserve it. Mercy is only needed by those who have no case.

verseByVerse.quote: All Israel has transgressed your law and turned aside, refusing to obey your voice. And the curse and oath that are written in the Law of Moses the servant of God have been poured out upon us, because we have sinned against him. He has confirmed his words, which he spoke against us and against our rulers who ruled us, by bringing upon us a great calamity. For under the whole heaven there has not been done anything like what has been done against Jerusalem. As it is written in the Law of Moses, all this calamity has come upon us; yet we have not entreated the favor of the LORD our God, turning from our iniquities and gaining insight by your truth. Therefore the LORD has kept ready the calamity and has brought it upon us, for the LORD our God is righteous in all the works that he has done, and we have not obeyed his voice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Law of Moses had set before Israel blessings for obedience and curses for disobedience, including defeat by enemies and exile from the land (Lev 26; Deut 28). Everything that had happened was written in advance. The exile was not a sign that God had lost control or broken his promises. It was proof that he keeps every word, including his warnings.

(The ESV notes that our rulers who ruled us can be translated "our judges who judged us".) The destruction of Jerusalem was unique because Jerusalem was unique. It was the city God had chosen for his name. The greater the privilege, the greater the fall.

This is one of the saddest sentences in the prayer. Even after the calamity fell, the people had not turned to God. Suffering alone does not change hearts; only God's grace does that.

Again Daniel says that God is righteous (see v. 7), and he will appeal to God's righteous acts in verse 16. He never accuses God. A man torn from his home as a boy insists that God was just in all of it.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, O Lord our God, who brought your people out of the land of Egypt with a mighty hand, and have made a name for yourself, as at this day, we have sinned, we have done wickedly. "O Lord, according to all your righteous acts, let your anger and your wrath turn away from your city Jerusalem, your holy hill, because for our sins, and for the iniquities of our fathers, Jerusalem and your people have become a byword among all who are around us. Now therefore, O our God, listen to the prayer of your servant and to his pleas for mercy, and for your own sake, O Lord, make your face to shine upon your sanctuary, which is desolate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now the prayer turns to request, and its first argument is history. God once brought his people out of slavery in Egypt with a mighty hand. That great rescue made God's name known among the nations. Daniel is asking God to do it again: a new exodus, this time from Babylon. The God who saved before can save again.

Daniel appeals to God's righteous acts. Here God's righteousness is not only his justice in punishing but also his faithfulness in saving, keeping his covenant promises. And he appeals to God's reputation. Jerusalem has become a byword, a joke among the nations. When God's people are disgraced, God's name is mocked.

Make your face to shine echoes the priestly blessing (Num 6:25). Daniel longs for God's favor to return to his ruined temple. And the ground of his plea is for your own sake. (The ESV notes that the Hebrew says "for the Lord's sake".) The great hope of every sinner is not what God owes us but what God owes to his own name. He will be true to himself.

verseByVerse.quote: O my God, incline your ear and hear. Open your eyes and see our desolations, and the city that is called by your name. For we do not present our pleas before you because of our righteousness, but because of your great mercy. O Lord, hear; O Lord, forgive. O Lord, pay attention and act. Delay not, for your own sake, O my God, because your city and your people are called by your name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This verse is the gospel in the Old Testament. We do not present our pleas before you because of our righteousness, but because of your great mercy. Daniel, one of the most righteous men who ever lived, brings only need and God's mercy. That is how every sinner must come. Not "accept me because I have tried hard", but "accept me because you are merciful". And the New Testament shows how a righteous God can be merciful to sinners without denying his justice. God put Christ forward as a propitiation by his blood, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Rom 3:25-26). In Christ, God's mercy and God's righteousness meet.

The prayer ends in short, urgent cries, the prayer of a man pouring out his heart, and it ends where it began: for your own sake, because the city and people bear God's name. Christians can pray this way too. We bear the name of Christ, and Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need (Heb 4:16).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gabriel comes while Daniel is still praying, with an answer sent at the prayer's first word (vv. 20-23).
verseByVerse.theology: God hears the prayers of his people from their first word, and he loves them.

verseByVerse.quote: While I was speaking and praying, confessing my sin and the sin of my people Israel, and presenting my plea before the LORD my God for the holy hill of my God, while I was speaking in prayer, the man Gabriel, whom I had seen in the vision at the first, came to me in swift flight at the time of the evening sacrifice. He made me understand, speaking with me and saying, "O Daniel, I have now come out to give you insight and understanding. At the beginning of your pleas for mercy a word went out, and I have come to tell it to you, for you are greatly loved. Therefore consider the word and understand the vision.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Daniel says my sin and the sin of my people. He confesses his own sin, not only the nation's. The holiest man in Babylon knew he was a sinner.

Gabriel, the angel of chapter 8, arrives at the time of the evening sacrifice. There had been no temple and no evening sacrifice in Jerusalem for nearly fifty years. But Daniel still marked the time of day when the lamb used to be offered. His heart kept the rhythm of worship even in exile. At that hour, God answered.

First, God answered at the beginning of Daniel's prayer, before he had finished speaking. God is not reluctant to hear his people. Jesus said, your Father knows what you need before you ask him (Matt 6:8).

Second, Gabriel tells Daniel, you are greatly loved. After a whole prayer of confessing sin and shame, heaven's reply begins by telling him he is loved. That is how God receives repentant sinners. Every believer in Christ can hear the same word. We are not loved because we deserve it but because God has set his love upon us in his Son.
verseByVerse.note: The evening sacrifice was offered in the afternoon; by New Testament times it was linked with the ninth hour.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers Daniel's seventy years with seventy weeks: a decreed time leading to an anointed one who will be cut off, to atone for iniquity and bring in everlasting righteousness (vv. 24-27).
verseByVerse.theology: God has decreed the time of the Messiah, who would be cut off to atone for sin and bring in everlasting righteousness.

verseByVerse.quote: "Seventy weeks are decreed about your people and your holy city, to finish the transgression, to put an end to sin, and to atone for iniquity, to bring in everlasting righteousness, to seal both vision and prophet, and to anoint a most holy place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Daniel had been thinking about Jeremiah's seventy years. God answers with seventy weeks. The word means "sevens". Most interpreters understand these as seventy sevens of years, that is, 490 years. Remember 2 Chronicles 36:21: the seventy years of exile made up for missed Sabbath years, which came every seventh year. Now God announces seventy times seven. The exile was nearly over, but a far greater problem remained. Seventy years in Babylon had not solved Israel's sin. A longer period, fixed by God, would lead to the real solution.

These seventy weeks are decreed: God has set the timetable. Their goal comes in six phrases. The first three deal with sin: to finish the transgression, to put an end to sin, and to atone for iniquity. The last three describe what God will bring in: everlasting righteousness, the fulfilment of vision and prophet, and the anointing of a most holy place.

Who could possibly do this? The temple sacrifices never put an end to sin. No return from exile brought in everlasting righteousness. These goals describe the work of Jesus Christ. He came to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself (Heb 9:26). He entered the holy places by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption (Heb 9:12). He is the fulfilment of all the prophets (Luke 24:44). And the ESV notes that a most holy place could also be "a most holy thing, or one". Many see here the anointing of Christ himself, the true temple, whom God anointed... with the Holy Spirit and with power (Acts 10:38).

How Jewish readers take it. Jewish interpreters usually read the seventy weeks as reaching from the destruction of the first temple to that of the second (a rabbinic count), and take the anointed ones of verses 25 and 26 as a Persian king, high priests or Judean rulers rather than the Messiah; the end of sacrifice is the fall of the temple in AD 70. So both readings agree that the weeks run up to Jerusalem's destruction by Rome. This commentary reads the anointed one who is cut off as Jesus, because only his death meets the goals of this verse, putting away sin by the sacrifice of himself (Hebrews 9:26).
verseByVerse.note: “Seventy weeks” is literally “seventy sevens.” Interpreters differ on how to count them; most Christian readers see their goal in Christ’s atoning work.

verseByVerse.quote: Know therefore and understand that from the going out of the word to restore and build Jerusalem to the coming of an anointed one, a prince, there shall be seven weeks. And for sixty-two weeks it shall be built again with squares and moat, but in a troubled time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seventy weeks are divided into three parts: seven weeks, sixty-two weeks and one final week (v. 27). The count begins with the going out of the word to restore and build Jerusalem. It runs to an anointed one, a prince. That is what the title Messiah means, and "Christ" is the same title in Greek. When Andrew met Jesus he said, We have found the Messiah (which means Christ) (John 1:41). The word was used of kings and priests who were anointed for their office, and above all of the promised King.

(The ESV notes another way of dividing the verse: "there shall be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks. It shall be built again". On that reading the anointed one comes after sixty-nine weeks.) This commentary takes that reading: the anointed one appears after sixty-nine weeks (483 years), and the counts below assume it. The accent marks added to the Hebrew by medieval scribes put a pause after the seven weeks; the KJV and many older translations read the two periods together. The KJV's unto the Messiah the Prince reads as a title; the Hebrew has no the, hence the ESV's an anointed one.

Which word to restore and build Jerusalem starts the count? Several decrees were issued by Persian kings. Cyrus allowed the Jews to return and rebuild the temple in 538 BC (Ezra 1:2-3). Artaxerxes sent Ezra to Jerusalem with broad authority in 458 BC (Ezra 7:11-13). And Artaxerxes allowed Nehemiah to rebuild the city walls in 445 or 444 BC (Neh 2:5). Many interpreters have noticed that if you count 483 years (sixty-nine weeks) from Ezra's commission in 458 BC, you arrive at about AD 26 or 27, when Jesus was baptized, anointed by the Spirit and began his public ministry. Others count from Nehemiah's commission, using a 360-day "prophetic year", and arrive at the days of Jesus' ministry and his entry into Jerusalem. Neither count is free of difficulty: the starting decree is debated, and the arithmetic should not be pressed to the day. But both lines of reckoning point to the time of Christ. The first is the simpler: it needs no special year, and it ends at the anointing of Jesus with the Spirit at his baptism, when the Anointed One appeared.

Meanwhile, Jerusalem shall be built again with squares and moat, but in a troubled time. Ezra and Nehemiah describe exactly that: rebuilding against opposition and fear.

verseByVerse.quote: And after the sixty-two weeks, an anointed one shall be cut off and shall have nothing. And the people of the prince who is to come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary. Its end shall come with a flood, and to the end there shall be war. Desolations are decreed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the long wait, the anointed one comes, and then he is cut off, a phrase used of being killed. The Messiah would not come to be served but to die. He shall have nothing, dying apparently without kingdom, followers or success.

Christians have long seen here the death of Jesus. Isaiah had said of the suffering Servant: who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living, stricken for the transgression of my people? (Isa 53:8). When Jesus hung on the cross, abandoned by his disciples, stripped of his clothes and mocked as a failed king, he truly had nothing. But by being cut off, he accomplished the very things verse 24 promised. (The KJV reads but not for himself; the Hebrew says literally "and nothing to him", which the ESV follows.)

Jerusalem and its rebuilt temple will be destroyed again. Jesus wept over Jerusalem and foretold it: they will not leave one stone upon another in you, because you did not know the time of your visitation (Luke 19:44). In AD 70, about forty years after the crucifixion, Roman armies under the general Titus did exactly that. The city that rejected its Messiah lost its temple, and it has never been rebuilt. (The ESV notes that Its end can also be read "His end".)
verseByVerse.note: On the traditional Christian reading, the anointed one cut off is Jesus in his death, and the destruction that follows is Jerusalem’s fall in AD 70.

verseByVerse.quote: And he shall make a strong covenant with many for one week, and for half of the week he shall put an end to sacrifice and offering. And on the wing of abominations shall come one who makes desolate, until the decreed end is poured out on the desolator."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The final week is the hardest part of the passage, and here Christians differ most. The key question is: who is he at the start of the verse?

Many in the Reformed tradition, and many Christians before them, believe he is the anointed one of verses 25-26, the Messiah. On this reading Jesus is the one who shall make a strong covenant with many, through his blood. At the Last Supper he said, this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins (Matt 26:28). And by his death, partway through that final week, he would put an end to sacrifice and offering. After his once-for-all sacrifice, the temple offerings had no more purpose, and within a generation they ceased forever. The one who makes desolate is then the Roman power that came against Jerusalem, and God's judgment will finally fall on the desolator too. Jesus spoke of the abomination of desolation spoken of by the prophet Daniel and linked it with the coming destruction of Jerusalem (Matt 24:15; Luke 21:20).

Many other Christians, especially dispensationalists (who read God's dealings with Israel and with the church as separate stages of history), believe he is the prince who is to come from verse 26, a future antichrist. On this reading the first sixty-nine weeks ended with Christ's first coming. Then there is a gap, the present church age, not counted in the prophecy. The seventieth week is still future: a seven-year period at the end of history, when the antichrist will make a treaty with Israel, break it halfway through, stop the temple sacrifices and set up an abomination, before Christ returns to destroy him. Its reasons deserve a hearing: the prince who is to come is the nearest person named before he; Jesus spoke of the abomination of desolation as still to come in his day (Matt 24:15); and the goals of verse 24 are not yet seen in full in the world.

A third reading, held by most critical scholars (who date the book's visions to about 165 BC), finds the whole prophecy in the second century BC. The anointed one cut off is the high priest Onias III, murdered about 171 BC; the prince who is to come is Antiochus IV (see chapter 8); the last half-week is the roughly three years in which he stopped the sacrifices and set up a pagan altar in the temple (11:31); and the most holy place is anointed when the temple is rededicated in 164 BC. Its strength is that chapters 8 and 11 describe Antiochus in similar words. Its weaknesses: 490 years from the exile overshoot the 160s BC by decades, and atonement and everlasting righteousness did not arrive in 164 BC. And some interpreters take the numbers symbolically, as a complete period stretching from the return from exile to the end of all things.

This commentary follows the first reading, because it best explains the six great goals of verse 24, needs no gap that the text itself does not mention, and fits the way the New Testament speaks of Christ's covenant and sacrifice and of Jerusalem's fall. But faithful Christians hold the other views, and we should hold our differences with humility. Nor should anyone use these weeks to set a date for Christ's return: of that day, Jesus said, no one knows (Matt 24:36). All Christians can agree on the most important thing: God decreed the time of the Messiah, who would be cut off, and through his death sin would be atoned for and everlasting righteousness brought in.

Think of where this chapter began. Daniel was praying about seventy years and a ruined city. God answered with the promise of a far greater deliverance: not only the return of exiles to Jerusalem, but the coming of the Anointed One who would deal with sin itself. But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son (Gal 4:4). And when Jesus began to preach, his first words were, The time is fulfilled (Mark 1:15).

9.title: Seventy Weeks
9.overview:
In the first year of Darius the Mede, Daniel reads in Jeremiah that Jerusalem's desolations will last seventy years (vv. 1-2).

He seeks God with fasting, confessing Israel's sin and God's justice (vv. 3-14), and pleads for the city and sanctuary on the ground of God's great mercy alone (vv. 15-19).

While he is still praying, Gabriel comes: the answer went out at the beginning of his prayer, for he is greatly loved (vv. 20-23).

Seventy weeks are decreed to deal with sin and bring in everlasting righteousness. An anointed one will come and be cut off, the city and sanctuary will be destroyed, and a strong covenant will be made with many for one week (vv. 24-27).
9.theology:
God's promises in Scripture do not make prayer unnecessary but move his people to pray with confidence (vv. 1-3; Jer 29:10-13).

True confession honors God's righteousness, owns sin without excuse, identifies with God's people and pleads only God's mercy and the honor of his name (vv. 4-19; Lev 26:40-42; Luke 18:13; Ezra 9:6; Neh 1:6).

God keeps every word he has spoken, both his warnings and his promises (vv. 11-14).

God hears his people from the first word of their prayer and receives repentant sinners as greatly loved (v. 23; Matt 6:8; Heb 4:16).

God decreed the time of the Messiah, who would be cut off to finish transgression, atone for iniquity and bring in everlasting righteousness (vv. 24-26; Isa 53:8, 12; Heb 9:12, 26; Rom 3:25-26; Gal 4:4; Mark 1:15).

Christ made the new covenant with many by his blood and ended the need for sacrifice; the city that rejected him was destroyed (vv. 26-27; Matt 26:28; Luke 19:43-44; 21:20; Matt 24:15).

Christians differ on the timing of the seventieth week and should hold their views with humility, while agreeing on the heart of the prophecy: the Messiah's atoning death (vv. 24-27).
9.examples: An old man reads Jeremiah, does the arithmetic and puts on sackcloth in the Persian capital. The most blameless man in Babylon prays "We have sinned" and pleads nothing but God's great mercy, at the hour of a sacrifice no longer offered. The answer is sent before he has finished, and it begins, "You are greatly loved." And at the end of the chapter stands an Anointed One, cut off, having nothing, and accomplishing everything.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Man Clothed in Linen
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After three weeks of mourning, Daniel sees a glorious man clothed in linen and falls to the ground, drained of strength (vv. 1-9).
verseByVerse.theology: Behind the events of history stands a glory that overwhelms human strength.

verseByVerse.quote: In the third year of Cyrus king of Persia a word was revealed to Daniel, who was named Belteshazzar. And the word was true, and it was a great conflict. And he understood the word and had understanding of the vision. In those days I, Daniel, was mourning for three weeks. I ate no delicacies, no meat or wine entered my mouth, nor did I anoint myself at all, for the full three weeks.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Chapters 10-12 are one long vision, the last and longest in the book: chapter 10 sets the scene, chapter 11 gives the message and chapter 12 closes it.

The date is about 536 BC. Two years earlier Cyrus had allowed the Jews to go home, that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled (Ezra 1:1). Many had returned to Jerusalem. Daniel had not. He was now probably in his eighties, still in Babylon or its region. The prayer of chapter 9 had been answered, but not all of God's people had gone home.

The word was true, and it was a great conflict. (The ESV notes that this could mean "it was about a great conflict".) The vision concerns war: wars between the kingdoms of the earth, and, as this chapter will show, a war in the unseen world behind them.

Daniel does not tell us exactly why he was mourning. But we know what was happening in Jerusalem at the time. The returned exiles had begun to rebuild the temple, and their enemies discouraged the people of Judah and made them afraid to build (Ezra 4:4). The great return was turning into a struggle. It may be that news of this reached Daniel and broke his heart.

His fast was partial. He gave up delicacies, meat, wine and the oil people used to refresh their skin. This sheds light on chapter 1. There, as a young man, Daniel refused the king's food and wine. Here, as an old man, he gives up meat and wine for a special season of mourning. So his lifelong habit was not to avoid them altogether. His refusal in chapter 1 was about that table and that king.

Is this the “Daniel fast”? Daniel fasted in mourning for his people, not for his health. The New Testament sets no diet for spiritual growth, and fasting is a voluntary humbling before God, done in secret (Matt 6:16–18). A simple diet adopted for prayer is fine; treating it as a spiritual formula is not.
verseByVerse.note: The third year of Cyrus was 536 BC. The Tigris (v. 4) was the great river east of Babylon.

verseByVerse.quote: On the twenty-fourth day of the first month, as I was standing on the bank of the great river (that is, the Tigris) I lifted up my eyes and looked, and behold, a man clothed in linen, with a belt of fine gold from Uphaz around his waist. His body was like beryl, his face like the appearance of lightning, his eyes like flaming torches, his arms and legs like the gleam of burnished bronze, and the sound of his words like the sound of a multitude.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The date is significant. The first month was the month of Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread, which ran from the fourteenth to the twenty-first day (Exod 12:18). Daniel's three weeks of fasting covered the very days when Israel celebrated its deliverance from Egypt. Far from Jerusalem, instead of feasting, he mourned and prayed. Three days after the feast ended, the answer came.

Linen was the clothing of priests and of heavenly beings; the belt of fine gold signals royalty. Daniel sees a figure of overwhelming glory. His body shines like a precious stone, his face flashes like lightning, his eyes blaze like torches, his limbs gleam like polished bronze, and his voice sounds like the roar of a crowd.

Anyone who knows the book of Revelation will recognize this description. John saw the risen Christ with eyes like a flame of fire, his feet were like burnished bronze, refined in a furnace, and his voice was like the roar of many waters (Rev 1:14-15). Because of this, many Christians believe the man clothed in linen was the Son of God himself, appearing before his birth in Bethlehem. Others believe he was a mighty angel, noting that the one who speaks to Daniel in verses 11-14 had to be helped by Michael against the prince of Persia, which seems unlike the Son of God. Some suggest that the glorious figure of verses 5-6 and the messenger of verses 10-21 are two different beings. The text does not settle the question, but this commentary judges the best reading to be that the glorious figure of verses 5–6 is the pre-incarnate Son, since John sees the same glory in the risen Christ, and that the angel who speaks to Daniel in verses 10–21 is another, a messenger who needs Michael's help. But whether we see Christ himself or a messenger reflecting his glory, the lesson is the same: behind the great conflict stands a Lord of unimaginable majesty.

verseByVerse.quote: And I, Daniel, alone saw the vision, for the men who were with me did not see the vision, but a great trembling fell upon them, and they fled to hide themselves. So I was left alone and saw this great vision, and no strength was left in me. My radiant appearance was fearfully changed, and I retained no strength. Then I heard the sound of his words, and as I heard the sound of his words, I fell on my face in deep sleep with my face to the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Daniel's companions saw nothing, but they felt something, and they ran. Something very similar happened when the risen Jesus met Saul on the road to Damascus: The men who were traveling with him stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one (Acts 9:7). God's presence can be real and terrifying even to those who do not see it.

Daniel is left alone. His strength drains away. The ESV notes that the Hebrew says "My splendor was changed to ruin". Whatever dignity and health he had as a great official of the empire collapsed in a moment. Before true glory, human glory disappears. Isaiah said the same when he saw the LORD: Woe is me! For I am lost (Isa 6:5).

Daniel collapses face down, overwhelmed into a kind of faint. People imagine meeting God with comfort and excitement; the Bible shows them falling down. We need to recover a sense of God's holiness. The one we worship is not a friendly idea but the glorious Lord of heaven.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–21 — Fear Not, Man Greatly Loved
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Touched and lifted, Daniel learns that his prayer was heard from the first day, though the answer was resisted by the prince of Persia, and he is strengthened to hear the message of the latter days (vv. 10-21).
verseByVerse.theology: Prayer is heard at once, even when the answer is delayed by a spiritual conflict God's people cannot see.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, a hand touched me and set me trembling on my hands and knees. And he said to me, "O Daniel, man greatly loved, understand the words that I speak to you, and stand upright, for now I have been sent to you." And when he had spoken this word to me, I stood up trembling. Then he said to me, "Fear not, Daniel, for from the first day that you set your heart to understand and humbled yourself before your God, your words have been heard, and I have come because of your words.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Step by step Daniel is raised. A hand touches him and lifts him to his hands and knees. Then a word lifts him to his feet. And the first thing he hears, as in 9:23, is that he is greatly loved. When the disciples fell on their faces at the transfiguration, Jesus came and touched them, saying, "Rise, and have no fear" (Matt 17:7). The God whose glory knocks us down is the God whose love lifts us up.

This is wonderful news for anyone who prays. Daniel's prayer was heard from the first day. God did not wait three weeks to listen. What delayed was the arrival of the answer, not God's attention.

The kind of prayer that was heard matters. Daniel set your heart to understand, seeking God's truth. And he humbled yourself before your God. God is near to those who seek him humbly. The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit (Ps 34:18).

verseByVerse.quote: The prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me twenty-one days, but Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me, for I was left there with the kings of Persia, and came to make you understand what is to happen to your people in the latter days. For the vision is for days yet to come."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why did the answer take three weeks? Because the prince of the kingdom of Persia resisted God's messenger for twenty-one days, exactly the length of Daniel's fast. Does that mean God was struggling to get through? No. The messenger was hindered, not God; the answer came at the time God appointed, and the hindrance was itself overcome by God's servant Michael. The delay was real, but it was never outside God's rule.

Here the curtain is pulled back on something the Bible rarely shows us. This prince cannot be the human king of Persia. No human king could hold back an angel from heaven. He is a spiritual being, an evil power working behind the empire of Persia. Against him comes Michael, one of the chief princes, a great angel. The New Testament calls him the archangel Michael (Jude 9), and Revelation shows Michael and his angels fighting against the dragon (Rev 12:7).

What does this mean for us? Paul says, we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places (Eph 6:12). The conflicts of history are not only political. There are spiritual powers at work behind nations and cultures, opposing God's purposes and God's people.

We should be careful not to go beyond what the Bible says. Scripture gives us very few details about these powers, and it never tells us to try to identify them, map them or speak to them. It tells us to pray, as Daniel did. And it tells us that Christ has already won the decisive victory: He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him (Col 2:15).

The purpose of the visit is to explain the future of Daniel's people in the latter days. That is the message of chapters 11 and 12.
verseByVerse.note: Michael is the archangel who guards Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: When he had spoken to me according to these words, I turned my face toward the ground and was mute. And behold, one in the likeness of the children of man touched my lips. Then I opened my mouth and spoke. I said to him who stood before me, "O my lord, by reason of the vision pains have come upon me, and I retain no strength. How can my lord's servant talk with my lord? For now no strength remains in me, and no breath is left in me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Once again Daniel is overwhelmed. He cannot speak.

A touch opens his lips, as the seraph touched Isaiah's lips so that he could speak (Isa 6:7). The messenger has the likeness of the children of man. He comes in a form Daniel can bear.

Daniel is honest about his weakness: no strength, no breath. He does not pretend to be a spiritual hero. And that is exactly the kind of person God strengthens. My power is made perfect in weakness (2 Cor 12:9).

verseByVerse.quote: Again one having the appearance of a man touched me and strengthened me. And he said, "O man greatly loved, fear not, peace be with you; be strong and of good courage." And as he spoke to me, I was strengthened and said, "Let my lord speak, for you have strengthened me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A third touch, and a word of peace. Fear not, peace be with you; be strong and of good courage. These words gathered up the encouragement God had given his servants for centuries. Joshua heard, Be strong and courageous. Do not be frightened (Josh 1:9). And the risen Jesus would stand among his frightened disciples and say, Peace be with you (John 20:19).

Daniel was not strengthened by trying harder. As he spoke to me, I was strengthened. God's word itself gave him strength. That is still how God strengthens his people, through his word. Daniel's response is the right one: Let my lord speak. Once he was strong enough to listen, he was ready to hear.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said, "Do you know why I have come to you? But now I will return to fight against the prince of Persia; and when I go out, behold, the prince of Greece will come. But I will tell you what is inscribed in the book of truth: there is none who contends by my side against these except Michael, your prince.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The messenger must go back to the fight. The spiritual power behind Persia is still resisting. And after Persia, the prince of Greece will come. As the kingdoms of the earth rise and fall, the unseen conflict moves on with them. Chapter 11 will show the earthly side of the same struggle.

The book of truth is God's own record of what will happen. The future is not uncertain to God. It is already written in his book. The Psalms say, in your book were written, every one of them, the days that were formed for me (Ps 139:16).

And Michael is your prince, the angel who has charge of Daniel's people (12:1). God's people are not alone in the conflict. Elisha once prayed for his frightened servant, and the young man saw the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha, and heard, those who are with us are more than those who are with them (2 Kgs 6:16-17).

For the Christian, the comfort is even greater. We are not only protected by angels. We belong to Christ, who has triumphed over every power. Little children, you are from God and have overcome them, for he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4). Nothing in this unseen war, nor angels nor rulers... nor powers, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord (Rom 8:38-39).

10.title: A Great Conflict
10.overview:
In the third year of Cyrus a true word is revealed to Daniel about a great conflict. After three weeks of mourning and fasting, he sees by the Tigris a man clothed in linen, whose glory leaves him without strength (vv. 1-9).

A hand lifts him: he is greatly loved, and his words were heard from the first day, though the messenger was withstood by the prince of Persia until Michael came to help (vv. 10-14). Touched and strengthened again, Daniel is ready to hear about the latter days, while the unseen battle goes on (vv. 15-21).
10.theology:
Mourning and humble prayer over the condition of God's people are pleasing to God (vv. 2-3, 12; Ps 34:18).

The glory of God and his messengers overwhelms human strength, and it foreshadows the glory of the risen Christ (vv. 5-9; Rev 1:13-17; Isa 6:5; Acts 9:7).

God lifts up those his glory has humbled, speaking love, peace and strength through his word (vv. 10-11, 18-19; Matt 17:6-7; Josh 1:9; John 20:19; 2 Cor 12:9).

Prayer is heard from the first day, even when the answer is delayed (v. 12; Luke 18:1).

Behind the nations are spiritual powers opposed to God, but God's angels contend for his people, and Christ has triumphed over every power (vv. 13, 20-21; Eph 6:12; Col 2:15; Jude 9; Rev 12:7; 2 Kgs 6:16-17).

The future is written in God's book of truth, and nothing can separate his people from his love (v. 21; Ps 139:16; 1 John 4:4; Rom 8:38-39).
10.examples: An old man fasts through the Passover season and sees, on the bank of the Tigris, a figure with a face like lightning; his companions see nothing and run anyway. Three touches lift the fallen man to his feet. His prayer was heard on the first day and answered three weeks later, because a spiritual prince stood behind an earthly empire. And the man who could not speak says at last, "Let my lord speak, for you have strengthened me."
