verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The messenger reveals the truth: three more kings will rise in Persia, and a fourth, far richer, will stir up all against Greece (vv. 1-2). Then a mighty king shall arise, but his kingdom will be broken and divided toward the four winds, not to his descendants (vv. 3-4).
verseByVerse.theology: God knows the course of empires before a single king is born.

verseByVerse.quote: "And as for me, in the first year of Darius the Mede, I stood up to confirm and strengthen him. "And now I will show you the truth. Behold, three more kings shall arise in Persia, and a fourth shall be far richer than all of them. And when he has become strong through his riches, he shall stir up all against the kingdom of Greece.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The messenger of chapter 10 is still speaking. He reminds Daniel that he has been active in the unseen conflict for some time. Since 10:21 has just mentioned Michael, him is probably Michael, whom the messenger supported, though some take it to mean King Darius.

Before we read this chapter, it helps to know what kind of chapter it is. It is one of the most detailed prophecies of history in the Bible. It describes, in advance, more than three hundred years of wars, marriages, betrayals and invasions. The names of the kings are not given, but the events match the history of the period so closely that readers have always been able to follow them. We do not need to memorize the details. The point is that God knew all of it before it happened, and that his people can trust him when the kings of the earth rage.

After Cyrus, three more Persian kings followed (Cambyses, the short-lived Bardiya and Darius I), and then a fourth who was enormously wealthy. This fits Xerxes I, who ruled from 486 to 465 BC and led a massive invasion of Greece in 480 BC. He is the King Ahasuerus of the book of Esther, who reigned from India to Ethiopia over 127 provinces (Esth 1:1). His invasion failed, and the conflict between Persia and Greece set the stage for what came next.

Does this detailed history show that the book was written after the events, about 165 BC? This is the main question about Daniel's date. Most critical scholars think so. Their reasons: the detail grows sharper as it reaches Antiochus IV in the 160s BC; verses 40-45 do not match how Antiochus actually died, which they take as a real prediction, made about 165 BC, that failed; and features of the book's Hebrew and Aramaic, with three Greek names of instruments in chapter 3, seem to them to fit a later time. Some of them also hold that detailed prediction cannot happen, but not all argue from that assumption. The case for the traditional date is also serious. The book presents these as Daniel's own visions (8:1; 9:2; 10:2), and Jesus speaks of the prophet Daniel (Matt 24:15). Copies of Daniel among the Dead Sea Scrolls were made within about a century of 165 BC, and the community that kept them already treated it as Scripture, which is hard to explain for a book only a few decades old. The Aramaic fits the official Aramaic used across the Persian empire, and names of instruments travelled early through trade. And verses 40-45, on this commentary's reading, are not a failed guess about Antiochus but a look beyond him (see v. 36). If God can tell the future, which Isaiah sets out as the very proof that he is God (Isa 46:9–10), detail is no difficulty. This commentary holds that Daniel received these visions in the sixth century BC, while saying plainly that the date is debated and that the evidence is argued both ways. The detail is what the angel says it is: the truth (v. 2) shown beforehand.
verseByVerse.note: Chapter 11 traces in detail the wars of the “kings of the north” (the Seleucids of Syria) and “of the south” (the Ptolemies of Egypt) after Alexander.

verseByVerse.quote: Then a mighty king shall arise, who shall rule with great dominion and do as he wills. And as soon as he has arisen, his kingdom shall be broken and divided toward the four winds of heaven, but not to his posterity, nor according to the authority with which he ruled, for his kingdom shall be plucked up and go to others besides these.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is Alexander the Great, the goat's great horn from chapter 8. More than a century after Xerxes attacked Greece, a Greek king overthrew Persia. He ruled a vast empire and could do as he wills.

As soon as he has arisen, he was gone. Alexander died young in 323 BC. His empire did not pass to his children, not to his posterity. His half-brother and his young son were both murdered within about fourteen years. His generals divided his lands among themselves, toward the four winds of heaven. Many are the plans in the mind of a man, but it is the purpose of the LORD that will stand (Prov 19:21).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–20 — Kings of the North and the South
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king of the south and the king of the north make and break marriage alliances, invade each other's lands and raise vast armies against one another (vv. 5-13). The king of the north stands in the glorious land, with destruction in his hand, but his schemes fail and he falls, and his successor is soon broken (vv. 14-20).
verseByVerse.theology: The plans of kings rise and collapse, and God's people live in the land between them.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then the king of the south shall be strong, but one of his princes shall be stronger than he and shall rule, and his authority shall be a great authority. After some years they shall make an alliance, and the daughter of the king of the south shall come to the king of the north to make an agreement. But she shall not retain the strength of her arm, and he and his arm shall not endure, but she shall be given up, and her attendants, he who fathered her, and he who supported her in those times.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the prophecy focuses on two of the kingdoms that came out of Alexander's empire, because they fought over the land of Israel, which lay between them. The king of the south means the Greek kings who ruled Egypt, the Ptolemies. The king of the north means the Greek kings who ruled Syria and the lands to the east, the Seleucids. For well over a century, Judea was the prize and the battlefield in their wars.

The first king of the south was Ptolemy I. One of his princes was Seleucus I, who had served as a commander under Ptolemy for a time and then built a far larger kingdom in the north.

About 252 BC the two kingdoms tried to make peace by marriage. The Egyptian princess Berenice was married to the northern king Antiochus II, who divorced his first wife to marry her. It ended in disaster. Within a few years Antiochus died, and Berenice, her young son and her attendants were murdered. Her father, the king of Egypt, had also died. Human peace treaties, sealed with marriages and promises, shall not endure.

verseByVerse.quote: "And from a branch from her roots one shall arise in his place. He shall come against the army and enter the fortress of the king of the north, and he shall deal with them and shall prevail. He shall also carry off to Egypt their gods with their metal images and their precious vessels of silver and gold, and for some years he shall refrain from attacking the king of the north. Then the latter shall come into the realm of the king of the south but shall return to his own land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Berenice's brother, Ptolemy III, came to the throne of Egypt, a branch from her roots. He invaded the northern kingdom to avenge his sister and won a great victory.

He returned to Egypt with enormous plunder, including images of gods. Once again the gods of the nations can do nothing. They are carried off in wagons by whoever wins the latest war.

The northern king, Seleucus II, later tried to strike back at Egypt but failed and went home.

verseByVerse.quote: "His sons shall wage war and assemble a multitude of great forces, which shall keep coming and overflow and pass through, and again shall carry the war as far as his fortress. Then the king of the south, moved with rage, shall come out and fight against the king of the north. And he shall raise a great multitude, but it shall be given into his hand. And when the multitude is taken away, his heart shall be exalted, and he shall cast down tens of thousands, but he shall not prevail. For the king of the north shall again raise a multitude, greater than the first. And after some years he shall come on with a great army and abundant supplies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sons of the northern king, Seleucus III and then Antiochus III, known as Antiochus the Great, raised huge armies and pushed south toward Egypt's frontier fortress.

In 217 BC, at the battle of Raphia near Gaza, the Egyptian king Ptolemy IV defeated Antiochus III and killed thousands of his soldiers. But his heart was exalted. Proud of his victory, he did not follow it up, and he shall not prevail. The win did not last.

Antiochus III did not accept defeat. He spent the next years campaigning in the east, rebuilding his power, and when the Egyptian king died and left a young child on the throne, he came back with a larger army than before. That is one reason God's people should never place their hope in the defeat of one tyrant. Another will rise. Our hope is in the kingdom that is not passed from hand to hand.

verseByVerse.quote: "In those times many shall rise against the king of the south, and the violent among your own people shall lift themselves up in order to fulfill the vision, but they shall fail. Then the king of the north shall come and throw up siegeworks and take a well-fortified city. And the forces of the south shall not stand, or even his best troops, for there shall be no strength to stand. But he who comes against him shall do as he wills, and none shall stand before him. And he shall stand in the glorious land, with destruction in his hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Egypt faced enemies on every side. And some of Daniel's own people, the violent among your own people, joined in, perhaps hoping to use the wars to win independence for Judea, as if they could make the prophecies come true by force. But they shall fail. Prophecy is not fulfilled by people trying to force it.

Around 200 BC Antiochus III defeated the Egyptians at Panium in the far north of Israel and then besieged their army in the fortified coastal city of Sidon until it surrendered.

As a result, the glorious land, Judea, passed from Egyptian control to the northern kingdom. Daniel's people now lived under a new master, and the stage was set for the terrible persecution to come.

verseByVerse.quote: He shall set his face to come with the strength of his whole kingdom, and he shall bring terms of an agreement and perform them. He shall give him the daughter of women to destroy the kingdom, but it shall not stand or be to his advantage. Afterward he shall turn his face to the coastlands and shall capture many of them, but a commander shall put an end to his insolence. Indeed, he shall turn his insolence back upon him. Then he shall turn his face back toward the fortresses of his own land, but he shall stumble and fall, and shall not be found.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Antiochus III tried to control Egypt through a marriage. He gave his daughter Cleopatra to the young Egyptian king Ptolemy V, hoping she would work for her father's interests. Instead she took her husband's side. The scheme shall not stand or be to his advantage.

Antiochus then pushed west into Asia Minor and Greece. There he met a new power: Rome. In 190 BC a Roman army under the commander Lucius Scipio crushed him at Magnesia and forced a humiliating treaty on him. (The ESV notes that the meaning of part of this verse is uncertain, but the general sense is clear.) Here Rome enters the story of this chapter, the power that on the traditional reading became the iron kingdom of chapters 2 and 7.

Weighed down by the fine Rome demanded, Antiochus went looking for money. In 187 BC he was killed while trying to plunder a temple in the east. The man once called "the Great" shall stumble and fall, and shall not be found.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then shall arise in his place one who shall send an exactor of tribute for the glory of the kingdom. But within a few days he shall be broken, neither in anger nor in battle.
verseByVerse.commentary: His son, Seleucus IV, needed money to pay Rome. He sent an official to collect taxes, and according to Jewish tradition this official even tried to seize the treasure of the temple in Jerusalem. Seleucus was later murdered by a plot, neither in anger nor in battle. The kings of the north keep grasping, and they keep falling.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A contemptible person to whom royal majesty has not been given seizes the kingdom by flatteries (v. 21). He deals deceitfully, wars against the south and sets his heart against the holy covenant (vv. 22-28); forced back by ships of Kittim, he profanes the temple and sets up the abomination that makes desolate (vv. 29-31). But the people who know their God shall stand firm and take action; the wise will teach many and suffer, and some will stumble so that they may be refined (vv. 32-35).
verseByVerse.theology: Persecution will come, but those who know God stand firm, and their suffering refines them.

verseByVerse.quote: In his place shall arise a contemptible person to whom royal majesty has not been given. He shall come in without warning and obtain the kingdom by flatteries. Armies shall be utterly swept away before him and broken, even the prince of the covenant. And from the time that an alliance is made with him he shall act deceitfully, and he shall become strong with a small people. Without warning he shall come into the richest parts of the province, and he shall do what neither his fathers nor his fathers' fathers have done, scattering among them plunder, spoil, and goods. He shall devise plans against strongholds, but only for a time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the prophecy slows down, because it reaches the man who matters most for Daniel's people: Antiochus IV, the little horn of chapter 8. He was contemptible, and the throne was not rightfully his. The rightful heir was his nephew, who was a hostage in Rome. Antiochus seized power through scheming and flattery.

The Bible's verdict is striking. This king called himself Epiphanes, "God made manifest". His coins called him divine. God calls him contemptible. The way God sees the powerful is often the exact opposite of the way they see themselves. And when God did make himself manifest, he came the other way: not seizing a throne by flattery, but emptying himself and taking the form of a servant (Phil 2:6-8).

The prince of the covenant may refer to the faithful high priest Onias III, whom Antiochus removed from office soon after he came to power, and who was later murdered. The man who held the highest office in God's covenant people was swept aside by a pagan king.

Antiochus made agreements and then broke them. And he rose to power with only a small people, a small band of supporters. Tyrants rarely begin with the backing of the many. A determined, deceitful few can seize a great deal of power when others are careless.

Antiochus was known for handing out plunder lavishly to buy loyalty, something his ancestors had not done. And the phrase that keeps returning in this chapter is here too: but only for a time. His plans have an expiry date set by God.

verseByVerse.quote: And he shall stir up his power and his heart against the king of the south with a great army. And the king of the south shall wage war with an exceedingly great and mighty army, but he shall not stand, for plots shall be devised against him. Even those who eat his food shall break him. His army shall be swept away, and many shall fall down slain. And as for the two kings, their hearts shall be bent on doing evil. They shall speak lies at the same table, but to no avail, for the end is yet to be at the time appointed. And he shall return to his land with great wealth, but his heart shall be set against the holy covenant. And he shall work his will and return to his own land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In 170-169 BC Antiochus invaded Egypt and defeated the young Ptolemy VI, who was betrayed by his own advisers, those who eat his food.

Antiochus and his defeated nephew sat down together, pretending friendship while each planned to deceive the other. They shall speak lies at the same table. What a contrast with the table of the Lord, where Christ gives himself in truth to his people. Yet even the lies of kings serve God's timetable: the end is yet to be at the time appointed.

On his way home, in 169 BC, Antiochus entered Jerusalem and robbed the temple of its treasures. His heart was now set against the holy covenant, against God's people and their worship.

verseByVerse.quote: "At the time appointed he shall return and come into the south, but it shall not be this time as it was before. For ships of Kittim shall come against him, and he shall be afraid and withdraw, and shall turn back and be enraged and take action against the holy covenant. He shall turn back and pay attention to those who forsake the holy covenant. Forces from him shall appear and profane the temple and fortress, and shall take away the regular burnt offering. And they shall set up the abomination that makes desolate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In 168 BC Antiochus invaded Egypt again. But this time ships of Kittim arrived. "Kittim" originally meant Cyprus and came to be used of peoples from across the western sea. Here it means Rome. A Roman fleet brought an ambassador who ordered Antiochus to leave Egypt. When the king asked for time to think, the Roman drew a circle in the sand around him and told him to decide before he stepped out of it. Humiliated, Antiochus withdrew.

He took out his rage on the Jews. He found allies among those who forsake the holy covenant, Jews who wanted to abandon their faith and live like Greeks. Persecution from outside is often helped by compromise inside.

In December 167 BC the daily sacrifices were stopped, and an altar to the Greek god Zeus was set up in God's temple, where unclean sacrifices were offered. This was the abomination that makes desolate, the outrage foretold in 8:11-13. Jesus later used the same phrase for a future desecration connected with the destruction of Jerusalem and the end (Matt 24:15). What Antiochus did became a pattern for later attacks on God's worship.
verseByVerse.note: Kittim (Cyprus/the West) refers to Rome, which forced Antiochus out of Egypt in 168 BC. He then set up an altar to Zeus in the temple.

verseByVerse.quote: He shall seduce with flattery those who violate the covenant, but the people who know their God shall stand firm and take action. And the wise among the people shall make many understand, though for some days they shall stumble by sword and flame, by captivity and plunder. When they stumble, they shall receive a little help. And many shall join themselves to them with flattery, and some of the wise shall stumble, so that they may be refined, purified, and made white, until the time of the end, for it still awaits the appointed time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the key verse of the chapter. Two kinds of people are named. Some violate the covenant, and the king wins them over with flattery, promises of position, safety and acceptance. Others are the people who know their God.

What makes the difference is not how much they know about God, but whether they know their God. Knowing God personally, the God who first made them his own, trusting him and loving him, is what enables believers to stand firm when the pressure comes. And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (John 17:3). And they take action. In 167 BC faithful Jews refused to sacrifice to idols, and a revolt began, led by a priestly family known as the Maccabees. Many refused to eat unclean food or abandon the law, even when it cost them their lives.

The wise are those who understand God's word, and they teach others. Faithful teaching is one of the great weapons of God's people in persecution. But the wise also suffer: by sword and flame, by captivity and plunder. Hebrews probably has faithful people of this period in mind when it speaks of those who went about in skins of sheep and goats, destitute, afflicted, mistreated— of whom the world was not worthy (Heb 11:37-38).

A little help probably refers to the military successes of the Maccabean revolt, which brought some relief. But it was only a little. The real deliverance of God's people would not come by the sword. And some who joined the cause did so insincerely, for their own advantage.

Why does God allow even the wise to fall? So that they may be refined, purified, and made white. Suffering is God's fire for purifying his people, the way a metalworker heats silver to remove its impurities. He will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver (Mal 3:3). Peter says the same to Christians: our trials come so that the tested genuineness of your faith—more precious than gold that perishes though it is tested by fire—may be found to result in praise and glory and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ (1 Pet 1:7). And even this suffering is limited: until the time of the end, the appointed time.

The temple Antiochus defiled was cleansed in 164 BC, and the Jews kept a yearly Feast of Dedication to remember it. John records that Jesus was in the temple at that very feast, walking in Solomon's colonnade, when he said, I and the Father are one (John 10:22-30). The house rescued from the contemptible king who called himself God made manifest was visited by the one in whom God truly came.
verseByVerse.note: Fulfilled in part in the Maccabean revolt; the temple was rededicated in 164 BC, remembered at the Feast of Dedication.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 36–45 — The King Who Exalts Himself
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: And the king shall do as he wills. He shall exalt himself and magnify himself above every god, and shall speak astonishing things against the God of gods (v. 36). He honors only the god of fortresses (vv. 37-39). At the time of the end he sweeps through the countries and camps near the glorious holy mountain, Yet he shall come to his end, with none to help him (vv. 40-45).
verseByVerse.theology: The last great enemy of God will exalt himself above all, and he will come to his end.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the king shall do as he wills. He shall exalt himself and magnify himself above every god, and shall speak astonishing things against the God of gods. He shall prosper till the indignation is accomplished; for what is decreed shall be done. He shall pay no attention to the gods of his fathers, or to the one beloved by women. He shall not pay attention to any other god, for he shall magnify himself above all. He shall honor the god of fortresses instead of these. A god whom his fathers did not know he shall honor with gold and silver, with precious stones and costly gifts. He shall deal with the strongest fortresses with the help of a foreign god. Those who acknowledge him he shall load with honor. He shall make them rulers over many and shall divide the land for a price.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With verse 36 we reach one of the most debated points in Daniel. Who is the king in verses 36-45?

Some believe the prophecy is still describing Antiochus IV. He did make great claims for himself and treated the gods of his fathers loosely. But the events of verses 40-45 do not match what we know of his last years. He did not conquer Egypt at the end of his life, and he did not die between the sea and Jerusalem. He died of illness in Persia.

Many others, including many in the Reformed tradition and most dispensational interpreters, believe that at this point the prophecy looks beyond Antiochus to the final enemy of God at the end of history, the little horn of chapter 7 and the man of lawlessness described by Paul. Antiochus was a preview of him, a small-scale picture of the final great rebellion. Paul seems to echo this very verse when he writes that the man of lawlessness exalts himself against every so-called god or object of worship... proclaiming himself to be God (2 Thess 2:4). The phrase At the time of the end in verse 40 also points in this direction. A third view, held by most critical scholars, keeps verses 40-45 about Antiochus and reads them as a prediction of his end that did not come true; but that reading depends on the late date it is used to prove, and it passes over the text's own signal that the horizon has moved. This commentary follows the second view, while recognizing that the line between Antiochus and the final enemy is not sharply drawn. The prophecy moves from the near horizon to the far one, the way a traveler sees nearby hills and distant mountains as one skyline.

Either way, the chief mark of this king is pride. He shall do as he wills. He exalts himself above every god. He speaks astonishing things against the God of gods. But he, too, is on a leash: He shall prosper till the indignation is accomplished; for what is decreed shall be done. God has decreed the limit.

He has no loyalty to any religion, only to himself. The one beloved by women is obscure. It may refer to a god especially popular with women in the ancient world, or to the natural desire for love and family, which this king despises. The main point is clear: he shall magnify himself above all.

The only god he truly worships is the god of fortresses: military power. Whatever he says he believes, his real trust is in force. And he buys loyalty by rewarding those who support him. It is a portrait of every godless tyrant, and of the final one.

verseByVerse.quote: "At the time of the end, the king of the south shall attack him, but the king of the north shall rush upon him like a whirlwind, with chariots and horsemen, and with many ships. And he shall come into countries and shall overflow and pass through. He shall come into the glorious land. And tens of thousands shall fall, but these shall be delivered out of his hand: Edom and Moab and the main part of the Ammonites. He shall stretch out his hand against the countries, and the land of Egypt shall not escape. He shall become ruler of the treasures of gold and of silver, and all the precious things of Egypt, and the Libyans and the Cushites shall follow in his train. But news from the east and the north shall alarm him, and he shall go out with great fury to destroy and devote many to destruction. And he shall pitch his palatial tents between the sea and the glorious holy mountain. Yet he shall come to his end, with none to help him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the time of the end, the conflicts of the past are repeated on a larger scale. The last enemy sweeps through the world like a whirlwind.

He enters the glorious land, the land of God's people, and conquers Egypt and its neighbors. Edom, Moab and Ammon, Israel's ancient enemies, escape him, perhaps because they side with him. Libya and Cush (the lands to the west and south of Egypt) follow him. The names are those of Daniel's world, but the picture is of a ruler who seems to hold all the wealth and power of the earth.

Then comes a sudden alarm. The picture recalls how God dealt with the Assyrian king Sennacherib long before: he shall hear a rumor and return to his own land (Isa 37:7). The conqueror turns in fury, and he sets up his royal camp between the sea and the glorious holy mountain, close to Jerusalem, where God's name dwells. It looks as though he is about to make his final attack on God's people.

And then, in a single sentence, it is over. Yet he shall come to his end, with none to help him. No battle is described. No army saves him. The one who helped his supporters (v. 39) has no one to help him. Paul says of the final enemy that the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and bring to nothing by the appearance of his coming (2 Thess 2:8).

That is the message of this long, difficult chapter. Kings plot, marry, betray, invade and plunder. Empires rise and fall. God's people suffer in the middle of it all. But every event was known to God before it happened, every enemy is given only a time, and the last and greatest enemy will come to his end. The LORD brings the counsel of the nations to nothing; he frustrates the plans of the peoples. The counsel of the LORD stands forever (Ps 33:10-11). Christ must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet (1 Cor 15:25). Until then, the calling of God's people is the calling of verse 32: to know our God, to stand firm and to act, not in our own strength but by the Spirit he has given us (Eph 6:10, 18).

11.title: The People Who Know Their God
11.overview:
The messenger reveals the truth: more Persian kings, then a mighty king whose kingdom is broken and divided toward the four winds (vv. 1-4).

The kings of the south and the north make and break alliances and wage war over the land between them (vv. 5-20).

A contemptible person takes the kingdom by flatteries, profanes the temple and sets up the abomination that makes desolate. Covenant-breakers are seduced, but the people who know their God stand firm and act, and the wise teach many and are refined by suffering (vv. 21-35).

The king exalts himself above every god and honors the god of fortresses. At the time of the end he sweeps through the countries and pitches his tents near the glorious holy mountain, yet he comes to his end with none to help him (vv. 36-45).
11.theology:
God knows the whole course of history in detail before it happens, and the plans of kings serve his purpose (vv. 2-35; Prov 19:21; Ps 33:10-11).

Human alliances, marriages and schemes cannot secure lasting peace or power (vv. 6, 17, 27).

God sees the proud as contemptible, whatever they call themselves (v. 21).

Persecution of God's people is aided by compromise within, but those who know their God stand firm and act (vv. 30, 32; John 17:3).

Faithful teachers strengthen God's people, and God uses suffering to refine and purify them for a limited, appointed time (vv. 33-35; Mal 3:3; 1 Pet 1:6-7; Heb 11:36-38).

The final enemy of God will exalt himself above every god, but he will come to his end, destroyed by the Lord Jesus at his coming (vv. 36-45; 2 Thess 2:4, 8; 1 Cor 15:25).
11.examples: A Persian king is rich enough to invade Greece, and a royal marriage meant to bring peace ends in murder. A small land is caught between two empires. A self-styled god, whom God calls contemptible, tells lies at the same table as his rival, is humiliated inside a circle drawn in the sand, and sets up an idol's altar in God's temple. And through it all, ordinary believers who know their God will not bow.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the final trouble God delivers everyone written in his book, and the dead awake, some to everlasting life and some to everlasting contempt (vv. 1-4).
verseByVerse.theology: History ends not in the grave but in resurrection, judgment and glory for those whose names are written in God's book.

verseByVerse.quote: "At that time shall arise Michael, the great prince who has charge of your people. And there shall be a time of trouble, such as never has been since there was a nation till that time. But at that time your people shall be delivered, everyone whose name shall be found written in the book.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The verse continues straight on from chapter 11: At that time is the final enemy's last attack, when he shall come to his end (11:45). First, Michael, the angel of 10:13, 21, arises: at the decisive moment heaven acts for God's people.

Second, there shall be a time of trouble, such as never has been. The final days will bring suffering greater than any before. Jesus took up these very words when he spoke of the end: For then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, no, and never will be (Matt 24:21). Christians understand this in different ways. Some, including dispensationalists, believe it describes a specific future period of great tribulation just before Christ returns. Many others, including many Reformed interpreters, believe the whole age between Christ's first and second comings is marked by tribulation for the church, rising to a final, terrible intensity before the end. This commentary takes the second view, though faithful Christians differ. Jesus says In the world you will have tribulation (John 16:33) and John calls himself a partner in the tribulation (Rev 1:9), and Jesus' own words in Matthew 24 speak first of Jerusalem's fall in AD 70 and then of the end. Both agree that believers should not be surprised by suffering, and that it will not have the last word.

Third, and most important, your people shall be delivered: everyone written in the book, God's book of life, the register of those who belong to him. Moses spoke of it (Exod 32:32). Jesus told his disciples, rejoice that your names are written in heaven (Luke 10:20). Revelation calls it the book of life of the Lamb who was slain (Rev 13:8), and the risen Christ promises the one who conquers, I will never blot his name out of the book of life (Rev 3:5).

This is the deepest comfort in the whole book of Daniel. When the worst comes, God's people will be kept not by their own strength or cleverness but because God has written their names in his book, and he does not lose what is his. I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:28).

verseByVerse.quote: And many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the clearest promise of the resurrection of the body in the whole Old Testament (Isaiah 26:19 comes close). Death is described as sleep in the dust of the earth. Since the fall, God's sentence on humanity has been you are dust, and to dust you shall return (Gen 3:19). But the dust is not the end. Those who sleep there shall awake.

Calling death "sleep" does not mean the dead are unconscious, or that death is unreal: it is still an enemy, and the last one to be destroyed (1 Cor 15:26). It means that death is not permanent. Sleep is followed by waking. That is why Paul could say to grieving Christians, we do not want you to be uninformed, brothers, about those who are asleep, that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope (1 Thess 4:13).

The resurrection divides humanity into two destinies, and the same word, everlasting, describes both. Jesus said the same: an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment (John 5:28-29). And he said, these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life (Matt 25:46).

What does everlasting contempt mean? It means that those raised to judgment are not put out of existence but go on, conscious, under the just and endless disgrace their rejection of God deserves. This commentary holds, with the historic church, that this punishment is conscious and everlasting, as the word shared with everlasting life suggests; some faithful Christians believe the wicked are finally destroyed, and they too take Scripture seriously. But no one should speak of this coldly. God says he has no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11). If you fear for someone you love, the door is open while life lasts, and Jesus turns away no one who comes to him (John 6:37). For he himself endured the cross, despising the shame (Hebrews 12:2), and bore that shame so that everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame (Romans 10:11).

Why does the verse say many rather than all? Some believe many here means the great multitude of the dead, that is, everyone, as Jesus' words suggest. Others think the verse focuses on the people of Daniel's own story, the faithful and the apostate of the final conflict. Either way, the rest of Scripture is clear that there will be a resurrection of both the just and the unjust (Acts 24:15).

This verse changes how we read the rest of Daniel. Many faithful people in this book were not rescued from death. The wise stumble by sword and flame (11:33); if this life were all, the persecutors would have won. But the martyrs will awake to everlasting life, and their persecutors to everlasting shame. And we know how this hope is secured: Jesus Christ has already risen from the dust. I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live (John 11:25).
verseByVerse.note: The clearest Old Testament statement of the resurrection of both the righteous and the wicked.

verseByVerse.quote: And those who are wise shall shine like the brightness of the sky above; and those who turn many to righteousness, like the stars forever and ever. But you, Daniel, shut up the words and seal the book, until the time of the end. Many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall increase."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who are wise are the faithful teachers of 11:33, who make many understand even when it costs them their lives. Despised and killed on earth, in the resurrection they will shine. The ESV notes that the sky above is literally "the expanse", the same word used in Genesis 1:6-8 for the sky God made on the second day of creation. Their glory will be as wide and bright as the heavens.

Jesus used the same picture: Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father (Matt 13:43).

The brightest are those who turn many to righteousness. Not the famous or powerful, but those who led others to God: a Sunday school teacher, a parent who prays with her children, a faithful pastor in a small church, a believer who quietly shares Christ with a friend at work: these are the ones who will shine like the stars forever and ever. Even now, Paul says, believers shine as lights in the world (Phil 2:15). One day the light will be complete.

Daniel is told to seal the book. As in 8:26, this means to preserve it securely, like a sealed legal document, not to hide it.

Run to and fro is often quoted as a prediction of modern travel and science. That is almost certainly not what it means. The prophet Amos used the same picture of people who shall run to and fro, to seek the word of the LORD, but they shall not find it (Amos 8:12). Here the idea seems to be that many will search anxiously for understanding in troubled times, and that, as history unfolds, knowledge of the meaning of Daniel's prophecy will grow. The sealed book becomes clearer as its words come true: the Jews under Antiochus understood more than Daniel (v. 8), and we, after Christ's coming, see further still. In the last book of the Bible, John is told the opposite of what Daniel was told: Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near (Rev 22:10). With the coming of Jesus, the end has drawn near.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Daniel asks how long, and is not given a timetable but a sworn promise, a blessing for those who wait, and rest in hope of the resurrection (vv. 5-13).
verseByVerse.theology: God's people are not given every date, but they are given a promise, and they wait, endure and rest in it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I, Daniel, looked, and behold, two others stood, one on this bank of the stream and one on that bank of the stream. And someone said to the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the stream, "How long shall it be till the end of these wonders?" And I heard the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the stream; he raised his right hand and his left hand toward heaven and swore by him who lives forever that it would be for a time, times, and half a time, and that when the shattering of the power of the holy people comes to an end all these things would be finished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The vision returns to the scene by the river where it began (10:4). Two more heavenly figures appear, perhaps as the two witnesses the Law required (Deut 19:15) to the oath about to be sworn.

The man clothed in linen of 10:5 stands above the waters. (The ESV notes this may mean he was "upstream".) One asks the question every suffering believer asks: How long?

The answer is given with a solemn oath. Raising not one hand but both, he swears by him who lives forever. Nothing could be more certain. Revelation echoes this scene, when a mighty angel raised his right hand to heaven and swore by him who lives forever and ever that there would be no more delay (Rev 10:5-6).

The length is a time, times, and half a time, the same limited period we saw in 7:25. (Some take it as three and a half literal years; others as a symbol of a limited time of trouble, half of a complete seven.) It is a real period of suffering, but it is measured, and it is broken off before it can become complete.

And the end will come when the shattering of the power of the holy people comes to an end. The end comes not when God's people are strongest but when their power has been completely broken. God often waits until his people have nothing left, so that the victory is plainly his. My power is made perfect in weakness (2 Cor 12:9). The same was true at the cross. When Jesus hung dead and his followers were scattered, the power of God's holy people seemed utterly shattered. Three days later, death itself was defeated.

verseByVerse.quote: I heard, but I did not understand. Then I said, "O my lord, what shall be the outcome of these things?" He said, "Go your way, Daniel, for the words are shut up and sealed until the time of the end. Many shall purify themselves and make themselves white and be refined, but the wicked shall act wickedly. And none of the wicked shall understand, but those who are wise shall understand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
How honest this is. After a lifetime of interpreting dreams and receiving visions, Daniel admits: I heard, but I did not understand. If Daniel did not understand, anyone who claims to have worked out every detail of prophecy should hold his theories with humility.

Go your way, Daniel is not a rebuke but a gentle release. Daniel does not need to understand everything. He needs to trust God and keep living faithfully. Jesus said something similar to his disciples when they asked about the timing of the kingdom: It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority (Acts 1:7). God has not given us a timetable to calculate. He has given us a promise to live by.

The coming troubles will have two opposite effects. Some will be purified by them, made white and refined like metal in the fire (11:35). Others will simply go on doing evil. The same suffering that sanctifies one person hardens another. Revelation says the same about the last days: Let the evildoer still do evil, and the filthy still be filthy, and the righteous still do right, and the holy still be holy (Rev 22:11).

And those who are wise shall understand. Understanding God's purposes is not a matter of intelligence but of faith. The wicked cannot understand because they will not submit to God. The wise understand because they fear him. The revelation of Jesus Christ, when it comes, will make everything clear to those who have waited for him (1 Pet 1:13).

verseByVerse.quote: And from the time that the regular burnt offering is taken away and the abomination that makes desolate is set up, there shall be 1,290 days. Blessed is he who waits and arrives at the 1,335 days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These two numbers are among the most puzzling in Daniel, and it is best to be honest: no one can be certain what they mean. Both numbers are a little longer than three and a half years (about 1,260 days, as in Rev 11:3). The first adds thirty days, and the second adds another forty-five.

Christians have understood them in several ways. Some apply them to the persecution under Antiochus IV, counting from the desecration of the temple to the end of that crisis. Some, especially dispensationalists, see them as extra periods after a future seven-year tribulation, perhaps for judgment and the setting up of Christ's kingdom. Others take the numbers symbolically, as a way of saying that the time of trouble may last a little longer than God's people expect, and they must keep waiting even when the end seems overdue. The first reading is the likeliest starting point, since the abomination and the taking away of the offering are Antiochus's acts (11:31); the persecution of his day then becomes a pattern of the last trouble, and the same call to wait applies to both.

Whatever the exact meaning, the verse puts its emphasis on one word: Blessed. Blessed is he who waits and arrives. The blessing does not go to the person who calculates the date. It goes to the person who waits faithfully and endures to the end. Jesus said, the one who endures to the end will be saved (Matt 24:13), and concerning that day and hour no one knows (Matt 24:36). The call of prophecy is not to predict but to persevere, and the God who wrote his people's names in his book is the one who keeps them to the end (v. 1; Phil 1:6).

verseByVerse.quote: But go your way till the end. And you shall rest and shall stand in your allotted place at the end of the days."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The book ends with a personal word to an old man who had been carried off as a boy, served four kings and two empires, faced lions, seen visions that made him sick and prayed for a city he would never see again. He is told three things.

Go your way till the end. Keep living faithfully for the time you have left. Daniel would not see the fulfilment of his visions. Like all the faithful of the Old Testament, he would die not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar (Heb 11:13).

And you shall rest. Daniel would die. But for the believer, death is rest from labor. Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on... that they may rest from their labors (Rev 14:13).

And shall stand in your allotted place at the end of the days. Daniel will rise again. He was one of those who sleep in the dust, and he will awake. And he will stand in his allotted place. When Israel entered the promised land, each family received its inheritance by lot (Josh 14:2). Daniel had lost his home in Judah. But God had kept an inheritance for him that no empire could take. The psalmist said, The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup; you hold my lot (Ps 16:5).

That promise belongs to every believer in Christ. We have been born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, to an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you (1 Pet 1:3-4). Jesus said, I go to prepare a place for you (John 14:2).

So the book that began with the fall of Jerusalem and a teenager carried off to Babylon ends with an old man told to rest in hope of the resurrection. In between, kings raged, empires rose and fell, and beasts made war on the saints, but the Most High ruled over all of it. The stone cut out by no human hand has begun its work. The Son of Man has received the kingdom. The Anointed One has been cut off for our sins and raised to life. And one day all who sleep in the dust will hear his voice. Until then, the word to Daniel is the word to every Christian: go your way, be faithful, and wait for him. The Lord Jesus says, Surely I am coming soon, and his church answers, Amen. Come, Lord Jesus! (Rev 22:20).

12.title: Those Who Sleep in the Dust Shall Awake
12.overview:
In a time of trouble unlike any before, Daniel's people will be delivered, everyone whose name is written in the book. Many who sleep in the dust will awake, some to everlasting life and some to everlasting contempt, and the wise will shine like the stars (vv. 1-4).

Asked how long, the man clothed in linen swears by him who lives forever: a time, times and half a time (vv. 5-7). Daniel does not understand and is told to go his way; blessed is the one who waits. He will rest and stand in his allotted place at the end of the days (vv. 8-13).
12.theology:
God delivers all whose names are written in his book, even through the greatest tribulation (v. 1; Matt 24:21; Luke 10:20; Rev 3:5; 13:8; John 10:28).

The dead will be raised bodily, some to everlasting life and some to everlasting shame, a hope secured by the resurrection of Jesus Christ (v. 2; John 5:28-29; 11:25; Matt 25:46; Acts 24:15; 1 Thess 4:13-14).

Those who are wise and turn many to righteousness will shine forever (v. 3; Matt 13:43; Phil 2:15).

God's word about the future is certain, sworn by him who lives forever, and his people's suffering is limited and ends when their own power is spent (vv. 6-7; Rev 10:5-6; 2 Cor 12:9).

Even prophets do not understand everything; God's people are called not to calculate dates but to wait, endure and be refined (vv. 8-12; Acts 1:7; Matt 24:13, 36; Rev 22:11).

Believers rest in death and will rise to receive the inheritance God has kept for them (v. 13; Heb 11:13; Rev 14:13; Ps 16:5-6; 1 Pet 1:3-4; John 14:2-3).
12.examples: God keeps a book with the names of his people written in it, and the graves are beds from which the sleepers will wake. A Sunday school teacher will shine like a star. An oath is sworn with both hands raised to heaven, and a great prophet says, "I did not understand." The blessing goes not to the one who calculates but to the one who waits, and the old exile is told to rest, promised a place of his own.
